articles.title: Here are 10 US tools you can replace right now with European alternatives | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Europe’s dependence on American technology can be found in the most everyday of places: in company inboxes, cloud infrastructure, analytics dashboards, team chats, shared documents, and increasingly in the AI tools employees use every day.
The numbers make that dependence difficult to ignore. According to Proton research published in February 2026, 73% of people surveyed across the UK, Germany and France believe their societies are far too dependent on US technology companies, and 83% of those respondents said they were concerned about that dependence.
But switching is not as simple as finding a company with a European address. A company can be European-founded but incorporated elsewhere; an EU-hosted product can still be owned by a non-European company; and a European SaaS company can depend heavily on American cloud infrastructure, payment rails or AI models.
Switzerland, Norway and the UK are European but not EU member states, with their own legal frameworks. So the list below should be treated as a starting point for procurement, not a sovereignty certification.
With that in mind, here are some of the everyday business tools companies can start reconsidering – and the European names worth putting next to them.
AWS, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud
This is a difficult one. Moving a social-media scheduler is an afternoon project; unwinding years of cloud architecture can be a company-wide programme. Amazon, Microsoft and Google also offer a breadth of managed databases, AI tooling, serverless products and developer services that few European providers replicate product-for-product.
There are nevertheless substantial European infrastructure companies to consider.
- Hetzner – Germany. Founded in 1997, Hetzner provides cloud servers, dedicated infrastructure, storage and hosting from a German company that also operates European data centres. It can be particularly compelling for businesses that need straightforward compute rather than hundreds of hyperscaler services.
- Internxt – Spain. Valencia-founded Internxt focuses on encrypted cloud storage and privacy-oriented digital services. It is worth considering for workloads centred on file storage and data management.
- IONOS — Germany. IONOS offers cloud infrastructure spanning virtual servers, storage, managed databases and Kubernetes, alongside dedicated servers and hosting. Its cloud platform is developed in-house, while the company operates data centres across Europe and North America. For businesses looking to reduce their reliance on AWS without giving up core infrastructure-as-a-service capabilities, IONOS is one of the more established European providers to consider.
- OVHcloud – France. Founded in 1999 and headquartered in Roubaix, OVHcloud is one of Europe’s most substantial home-grown cloud infrastructure providers, spanning public and private cloud, bare metal, storage and hosting. Of the options here, it comes closest to the profile of a large European infrastructure player.
- Scaleway – France. Part of French telecoms group Iliad, Scaleway offers public cloud, compute, object storage, databases, Kubernetes and dedicated infrastructure. It is another credible option for teams that want to move core cloud workloads under a European provider.
- STACKIT – Germany. STACKIT grew out of the infrastructure needs of Schwarz Group, the German group behind Lidl and Kaufland, and is now part of Schwarz Digits. It operates European data centres and explicitly positions itself around cloud sovereignty and organisational independence.
ChatGPT
Europe’s AI question is particularly complicated because even a European-facing application can sit on models, chips or infrastructure originating elsewhere. Nevertheless, there are European companies building meaningful parts of the AI stack.
- Lovable – Sweden. Stockholm-based Lovable allows users to create applications and websites through natural-language instructions. It is one of Europe’s fastest-growing AI startups, but there is an important product distinction: Lovable is primarily an AI software-building platform, not a general-purpose conversational assistant. It may replace some ChatGPT workflows around prototyping and coding, but not ChatGPT as a whole.
- Mistral AI – France. Paris-based Mistral is the most obvious European name for businesses examining alternatives in generative AI. Its platform covers models, assistants, agents and enterprise deployments, while the company has increasingly framed its expansion around European control of AI infrastructure and the wider value chain.
- Lumo – Switzerland. Developed by Proton, Lumo is a privacy-focused AI assistant designed much more directly as an alternative to products such as ChatGPT. Proton says conversations are protected by zero-access encryption and are not used to train models.
Cloudflare
Cloudflare has become one of those pieces of internet infrastructure that many businesses barely think about until something goes wrong.
- BlazingCDN – Poland. BlazingCDN is a Polish content-delivery provider with a network designed for distributing digital content internationally.
- bunny.net – Slovenia. bunny.net has grown from CDN services into a broader edge platform covering delivery, storage, security and compute. Its network now spans multiple continents while the company remains European-based.
- KeyCDN – Switzerland. KeyCDN is operated by privately funded Swiss company proinity LLC and provides global content-delivery infrastructure.
- Myra Security – Germany. Munich-based Myra Security combines CDN services with security products including DDoS protection and web application security, making it particularly relevant for organisations where Cloudflare is doing more than simply accelerating static files.
Dropbox
File storage is one of the categories where Europe has a healthy range of alternatives, from simple synchronisation products to heavily privacy-focused encrypted services.
- Filen – Germany. Filen provides end-to-end encrypted cloud storage and says both its headquarters and servers are located in Germany.
- Koofr – Slovenia. Koofr is a Slovenian cloud-storage provider offering file syncing, sharing and encrypted storage, with data stored in EU-based data centres.
- pCloud – Bulgaria. pCloud is a cloud-storage provider covering file synchronisation, sharing and encrypted-storage options.
- Proton Drive – Switzerland. Proton Drive provides end-to-end encrypted cloud storage from Proton’s Swiss ecosystem and is increasingly aimed at both individuals and business customers.
Gmail
Email is a particularly sensible place to reduce concentration risk because moving providers is possible without asking every client, supplier and employee to join the same new network. Owning the company’s domain also makes future migration considerably easier.
- mailbox – Germany. Berlin-based mailbox.org offers business and personal email alongside cloud, office and meeting tools, positioning itself around privacy and GDPR-compliant European working environments.
- Posteo – Germany. Posteo is an independent Berlin email provider with a longstanding focus on privacy, ad-free email and data minimisation.
- Proton Mail – Switzerland. Proton’s encrypted email service offers both individual and business accounts.
- Soverin – Netherlands. Amsterdam-based Soverin focuses on paid, privacy-oriented email hosting, including custom-domain email for users who want to retain control of their address if they later change provider.
- Tuta – Germany. Tuta is a German encrypted email and calendar provider offering consumer and business products, including support for custom domains.
Google Analytics
Analytics is another area where switching can do more than change the flag on the invoice. Several European providers have built their products around collecting less personal data in the first place.
- Piwik PRO – Poland. Piwik PRO is an analytics platform combining web and app analytics with tools including consent and tag management. It is particularly positioned towards organisations that need deeper analytics while operating under demanding privacy or compliance requirements.
- Plausible Analytics – Estonia. Plausible is built by a European team and currently hosts visitor data exclusively using European-owned infrastructure. The company has also made its infrastructure choices unusually transparent, listing Hetzner in Germany, UpCloud in Finland and bunny.net in Slovenia among the providers it uses.
- Simple Analytics – Netherlands. Founded in Amsterdam, Simple Analytics provides privacy-focused web analytics without attempting to reproduce every layer of Google Analytics complexity.
Google Calendar
Calendars contain a revealing map of a company: who is meeting whom, when teams are travelling, which clients are being visited and what senior staff are working on. There are European alternatives ranging from straightforward shared calendars to encrypted services.
- Calendar.online – Germany. Based in Düsseldorf, Calendar.online provides shared calendars, permissions and booking functions, with servers located in Germany.
- fruux – Germany. Münster-based fruux provides calendar and contact synchronisation using open standards including CalDAV and CardDAV, which can also make it attractive to companies worried about lock-in.
- Proton Calendar – Switzerland. Proton Calendar brings the company’s privacy-first approach to scheduling, with Proton incorporated and headquartered in Switzerland.
- Tuta Calendar – Germany. Tuta’s encrypted calendar is hosted in Germany and forms part of the wider Tuta email and productivity ecosystem.
Google Docs
Shared documents are where network effects become particularly noticeable. Sending someone a different storage link is easy; changing how an entire organisation writes, comments, shares and edits together takes more planning.
- Infomaniak kDrive – Switzerland. Infomaniak combines storage and collaboration in kDrive. The company says the service is developed and hosted exclusively in Switzerland and integrates collaborative office tooling.
- Nextcloud Office – Germany. Stuttgart-based Nextcloud has made digital sovereignty a core part of its positioning. Nextcloud Office provides collaborative document editing within a Nextcloud environment, allowing organisations to self-host or select their own infrastructure rather than automatically placing files with a single SaaS provider.
- Nuclino – Germany. Nuclino is a collaborative document and knowledge-management platform, offering a lighter-weight option for teams that want shared documents, wikis and internal knowledge in the same workspace.
- Proton Docs – Switzerland. Docs in Proton Drive offers real-time collaborative editing with end-to-end encryption, including sharing and collaboration functionality for teams.
Microsoft Teams or Slack
This may be one of the hardest cultural migrations on the list. The technical alternatives exist; convincing every department to stop sending “quick Slack messages” is another matter.
- Fleep – Estonia. Tallinn-founded Fleep combines team messaging, tasks, file sharing and email interoperability. One limitation is worth noting for Teams users: Fleep does not provide native audio and video calls in the same way as a full Teams deployment, relying instead on integrations for calling.
- Infomaniak kChat – Switzerland. kChat is Infomaniak’s team-messaging product within kSuite, providing channels and workplace communication from the provider’s infrastructure.
- Nextcloud Talk – Germany. Nextcloud Talk combines chat, audio and video conferencing with an architecture that can be hosted on an organisation’s own infrastructure or with a chosen provider. That makes it particularly interesting for companies that want technological control rather than simply another SaaS subscription.
- Stackfield – Germany. Munich-based Stackfield combines team communication, project management, files and conferencing in one platform. The company says its servers are in Germany and explicitly markets the product to European organisations handling sensitive information.
- Whereby – Norway. Whereby is a European-owned video-meeting company focused on browser-based calls and embedded video. It is a strong candidate for the meeting side of Teams, although it is not a complete replacement for Slack-style persistent workplace messaging on its own.
Notion
Notion has become the miscellaneous drawer of the modern company: wiki, notes, project tracker, database, meeting archive and sometimes a makeshift CRM. Europe has several interesting products approaching that workspace from very different directions.
- Anytype – Switzerland. Anytype is a local-first workspace for notes, documents, projects and knowledge management, with a strong emphasis on user control and encrypted data.
- Craft – Hungary. Founded by Hungarian entrepreneur Bálint Orosz, Craft grew out of Budapest and focuses on documents, notes and collaborative knowledge work.
- Supernotes – United Kingdom. London-based Supernotes takes a different approach to knowledge management, organising information into collaborative Markdown notecards rather than attempting to recreate Notion’s database-heavy structure.
A European technology stack does not have to go through one dramatic “delete everything American” weekend.
For most companies, that would be expensive, disruptive and probably counterproductive. A more realistic approach is to identify the systems where concentration creates the greatest operational or strategic risk, then replace them one layer at a time.
Europe does not lack software companies capable of providing everyday business tools. What it has lacked is the habit of putting them on the procurement shortlist.
For companies serious about digital sovereignty, this shortlist is a good place to start.

articles.title: The wearable future is stuck in weird, experimental, existential limbo
articles.text:
This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.
The wearable future is stuck in weird, experimental, existential limbo
I sat down with Google to discuss its vision for the next generation of wearables. It’s a work in progress.
The wearable future is stuck in weird, experimental, existential limbo
I sat down with Google to discuss its vision for the next generation of wearables. It’s a work in progress.
For the past week, I’ve been testing the Google Pixel Watch 5. In many ways, it’s a typical, modern smartwatch. In others, it feels like one part of a wearable future that’s increasingly in flux. Everyone I’ve spoken to in wearable tech has roughly the same goal — soon, your tracker of choice will feature a helpful AI coach, “check engine” alerts that preventively flag hard-to-detect health conditions, and personalized health recommendations based on your lived experiences and needs.
That’s certainly what’s being pitched. But so far, it seems like most companies don’t know how exactly we’re going to get there.
AI coaches? Even the best ones are too chatty, fixate on one random detail you shared during setup, and require a ton of hand-holding. “Check engine” alerts can be useful and have been documented as saving lives. They can also spark health anxiety and the regulatory quagmire can be expensive to navigate. Personalized health holds great promise, but requires so much of your private data while also being subject to AI’s myriad shortcomings. Even now, most people think of wearable devices as fancy step trackers.
“Historically, wearables have been very focused on hardcore health enthusiasts,” Rishi Chandra, Google’s vice president of health and home, tells me at a roundtable of tech reporters in New York ahead of Made by Google. Usually, tech companies like to keep mum on future ideas and plans. But recently, Google seems eager to lay out its particular vision.
“There’s a huge market of people who are not thinking about their health every day. Today, wearable penetration is about 30 percent — 70 percent of the population has no notion of wearables,” Chandra adds.
In other words, wearable tech is still in its early days with a lot of untapped potential. The smartwatch is not the end-all, be-all. The fact that wearables can also capture a vast array of personal data compounds that. That’s one reason why, during last year’s Made by Google event, Chandra and Sandeep Waraich, Google’s senior director of wearables, told me that the future of AI gadgets won’t just be a single device. It’ll be an entire ecosystem of diverse accessories.
Since that chat, I’ve already seen several signs supporting Google’s multi-wearable ecosystem thesis. Multiple companies have pivoted to AI glasses (or as Google calls it, “intelligent eyewear”). But we’ve also seen other wearable form factors start gaining steam. See: the horde of screenless Whoop dupes and smart rings. In the AI sphere, some wearable makers are eschewing the health tracking aspect altogether. Some smart jewelry startups like Vocci, Taya, and Sandbar envision rings and pendants as a way to record and transcribe your thoughts using AI.
These are not proven ideas. That there are so many different approaches is a pretty big indication that the entire industry is in the process of throwing wearable spaghetti at a wall, desperately hoping that something will stick and be the next smartphone. It’s enough to make a senior wearable reviewer excited — because yay! Weird experimental products — and also mad — because no! Weird experimental products that don’t work as advertised! Still, there’s a nugget of truth in this new search for new wearable form factors and use cases.
“Wearables are a great conduit for presence. And it goes both ways. As AI reaches you in a respectful way, and as you want to interact with it, these interactions will become more frequent, but also quicker and glanceable,” says Waraich, noting that Google views seven seconds as its current benchmark for any one wrist-based interaction. The question now is figuring out the ideal surface for each specific technological task. For example: What device should you use to check your calendar? Your phone, tablet, or laptop? Or, with the addition of the Proactive Assistance feature on the Pixel Watch 5, should it be your smartwatch?
According to Chandra and Waraich, Google has had deep internal discussions about the pros and cons of various wearable form factors. Smart rings, for instance, are something that Google consistently gets asked about but won’t be pursuing in the short term.
“To be clear, we’re not closing the door on [smart rings],” Chandra says. “But our belief right now is that there’s so much headroom on a wrist-worn wearable … I think the Fitbit Air is going to have far bigger expansion opportunities given how simple and easy it is for everyone to use it.”
Okay, so Google just introduced the minimalist Fitbit Air and for now is passing on smart rings. Perhaps then the next step is an “Ultra” Pixel Watch as Samsung and Apple have done. Not so. When I ask, Waraich explains the current Pixel Watch is where Google sees its premium offerings. Chandra adds that the company is wary of spreading itself too thin.
Google certainly has a hypothesis of what wearable tech ought to be. It’s placing its bets through product launches and software updates, watching carefully to see how we — the wearable lab rats — react to specific ideas. The experiment continues.
Another wearable debate: whether it makes sense to add in microphones just because you can. For example, putting mics in something like the Fitbit Air so that it can also double as your AI memory — something akin to Amazon’s Bee device.
“At this point, it’s not a technology issue. It’s a user-sentiment, privacy issue. If you [add] a mic, it’s not just that it’s learning from you. It’s learning from the environment. So I think we’re being cautious about how to push that in the right way,” Chandra says, noting it’d have been easy for Google to stuff microphones into the Fitbit Air but the actual problem is whether doing so would add any customer value. “I don’t know yet if we have, as a tech industry, have figured out the right balancing act there.”
Having tested several AI wearables, my answer is a resounding hell no. As I’ve written on the site, this type of AI wearable tech often makes me feel like a spy. Similarly, I’ll simply point to the defunct Amazon Halo trackers, which not only tracked your emotions based on the tone of your voice but also created highly cursed, self-esteem-obliterating 3D models of your body to estimate fat percentages. Just because AI wearables can track new things doesn’t mean they should.
This problem also plagues smart glasses, as seen with the recent privacy backlash toward Meta’s “pervert glasses.” Some of that is Meta’s penchant for sticking its foot in it. Some of that, Google argues, is perhaps a matter of time and place. Perhaps, Chandra notes, people are more amenable to ambient computing — where your devices are always listening — inside the home instead of outside of it.
Even so, Google is committed to experimenting. What if, Waraich posited, the camera in smart glasses simply acted as a sensor without recording? As in, the glasses see what you see and can answer questions about your environment, but nothing gets recorded for posterity. In theory, this might mean the ability to automatically log your food without ever having to take a picture. A blind person might be able to ask an AI questions about their surroundings, and passersby wouldn’t have to worry that a photo of them exists in someone else’s camera roll.
To that, I say: Love the concept, good luck communicating how that’s different to the masses.
This is part of the existential problem facing my beat. How can any AI wearable be versatile enough to account for every individual’s privacy preferences and health journey? It’s easy enough to differentiate the hardware. Casual users? You get a Fitbit Air or Oura Ring. Tech nerds tired of their phones? Depending on your phone, I’ll point you to a Pixel Watch or Apple Watch. Oh, you’re entering an Ironman? I already know you’re wondering which flavor of Garmin or Coros suits you best.
But the software experience is a whole ’nother beast. Right now you can pick from multiple wearable form factors, but they all pretty much give you the same cluttered app and whap you over the head with data fatigue. That’s hardly a recipe for personalized health. I’ve shared over the course of several Optimizers that my current health journey relates to fixing my borked metabolism. That requires one set of advice. A cancer patient would need something wholly different. So would a hypochondriac or a young college athlete. Maybe you like a drill-sergeant-type coach. Or, if you’re like me, that type of tough love would make you want to throw up your hands. It’s already hard enough for people to learn how to be wise and judicious about their health, to accept limits and practice compassion without veering into overindulgence. How the hell can any one LLM achieve that wisdom? How can we expect one cluttered, unified software experience to meet the needs of an infinite number of individual needs?
I asked both Chandra and Waraich this. Both were optimistic that AI will one day get there, but it isn’t there currently. They acknowledged that this is a yearslong journey that will require lots and lots of work. That there are a lot of societal and cultural questions that’ll have to be debated internally and externally. After a decade, my wearable bullshit radar is strong, and since Wear OS 3, Google has genuinely welcomed a good wearable grilling whenever I (or other reporters) have offered frank feedback. I can’t say the same for every gadgetmaker on my beat.
I also can’t tell whether Google’s making all the right wearable bets with the Pixel Watch 5, Fitbit Air, or its AI coach. Maybe it’s a whiff to pass on smart rings. I still think I need to see more proof that an AI hardware ecosystem of diverse accessories is the ultimate move. I’ll give Google credit for being so candid about the multiple layers of privacy, culture, design, and tech logistics that go into the current era of wearable gadgets. That said, whenever I zoom out, I can’t help but feel like I’m caught in the proverbial hamster wheel. Testing each new smartwatch, smart ring, or smart glasses, I keep running toward this vaguely defined, AI-powered wearable future. I just don’t feel any closer to reaching it.

articles.title: Seasonic Readies First 80 Plus Ruby Certified Consumer PSU
articles.text:
Wednesday, August 19th 2026
	
		
	
	
	
Seasonic Readies First 80 Plus Ruby Certified Consumer PSU
Seasonic has become the first manufacturer to earn 80 Plus Ruby certification for an ATX power supply tested at 115 V. The Seasonic PRIME ENTERPRISE RX-1600, a high-wattage ATX power supply designed for demanding desktop, workstation, and AI systems, meets the program's highest efficiency tier. Seasonic has a long history of firsts in the 80 Plus program. In 2005, Seasonic became the first power supply manufacturer to certify products under the program's rigorous criteria with the Seasonic SS-400HT, and the first to bring a complete family of four certified products to market that same year. In 2008, Seasonic was again the first to achieve 80 Plus Gold certification. The Ruby milestone continues that legacy.
"Seasonic has been involved with 80 Plus since the program's launch, so this result is significant for us, said Walter Sun, CEO of Seasonic. Our first certified PC power supply appeared in 2005, followed by the first Gold certification in 2008," said a Seasonic representative. "Reaching Ruby at 115 V reflects the continued focus on efficiency in our engineering work. We are at a point where every additional percent of efficiency is difficult to achieve, but the effort is worthwhile because these small gains translate into enormous savings on a global scale."Ruby is the newest and most demanding tier in the 80 Plus program, which is administered by CLEAResult. To earn Ruby certification, a power supply tested at 115 V must achieve:
Meeting these targets requires advances across the full platform, including switching control, thermal design, component selection, and validation. Modern desktop systems, workstations, and AI-oriented configurations place sudden, high-amplitude load swings on the power supply. Higher conversion efficiency reduces energy lost as heat and reduces cooling requirements—an advantage that becomes increasingly important in denser, large-scale installations.
"Ruby sets a new standard for what high-performance power supplies can achieve, including efficiency at low load—which is where most systems spend the majority of their time," said Jeremy Townsend, Senior Vice President, Delivery Services, CLEAResult.
"Seasonic has been part of the 80 Plus program since the beginning, and this milestone reflects what the program was designed to drive: real efficiency improvements that reduce energy waste and lower costs for businesses and consumers. We expect Ruby to help set the pace for what manufacturers will be working toward heading into 2027. Congratulations to Seasonic for this achievement.
Ruby is the latest step in Seasonic's continued push for efficiency and engineering excellence. As with earlier platforms, the goal remains to combine high efficiency with stable electrical performance, effective thermal management, and long-term reliability.

articles.title: PV-Modul nutzt Weltraum-Kälte: Heizen, Kühlen und Strom erzeugen auf einer Fläche
articles.text:
Heizen, kühlen, Strom erzeugen: Dieses Solarsystem macht gleich 3 Dinge auf einmal
Auf Dächern und an Fassaden ernten PV-Module schon lange Sonnenenergie für eine grüne Stromproduktion. Künftig könnte auf der gleichen Fläche auch noch Wärme und Kälte aus erneuerbaren Quellen erzeugt werden. Das passende System dafür entwickeln Forschende um Gan Huang vom Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT). Feldtests eines Prototypen verliefen erfolgreich, wie sie kürzlich in der Fachzeitschrift Cell Reports Physical Science berichteten.
Das neuartige Modul kombiniert Solartechnologie mit einem System zur sogenannten passiven Strahlungskühlung. Eine lichtdurchlässige Schicht auf dem Modul sendet dabei Wärme als Infrarotstrahlung ins kalte All. An dieser grünen Kühltechnologie arbeiteten Forschende weltweit schon seit Jahren und mit unterschiedlichsten Materialien.
„Auch die Kälte des Weltraums ist eine erneuerbare Ressource. Wenn wir lernen, die heiße Sonne und die Kälte des Weltalls gemeinsam zu nutzen, können wir eine neue Generation von Energiesystemen erschließen“, sagt Huang. Die Forschenden sehen entsprechende Module künftig nicht nur auf Dächern und Fassaden. „Das Konzept könnte auch für energieintensive Anwendungen wie KI-Rechenzentren interessant sein, die viel Strom und Kühlung benötigen“, so der Forscher.
Das kalte Weltall als Wärmefalle nutzen
Das Kernstück des Systems ist eine dünne Siliziumdioxidplatte, die mit dem Silikon Polydimethylsiloxan (PDMS) beschichtet ist. Die Kombination lässt Sonnenlicht nahezu ungehindert hindurch und gibt zugleich Wärmestrahlung in einem Wellenlängenbereich ab, der nicht von Treibhausgasen wie Kohlendioxid oder Wasserdampf geschluckt wird. Physiker nennen ihn „atmosphärisches Fenster“.
Hinter dieser kühlenden Schicht wird das Sonnenlicht über eine Linse auf einen kleinen Sonnenkollektor fokussiert. Dort entstehen Strom und Wärme, die in ein Stromnetz beziehungsweise Heizsystem eingespeist werden können. Die Trennung der gegensätzlich wirkenden Systeme sei die größte Herausforderung gewesen, heißt es. „Wir bringen ‚Feuer‘ und ‚Eis‘ zusammen“, so Huang.
Der Prototyp des Hybridsystems blieb in Freilandversuchen bis zu sechseinhalb Grad Celsius kälter als die Umgebung. Gleichzeitig liefert er eine elektrische Leistung von rund 60 Watt pro Quadratmeter und – für eine Wärmenutzung – Temperaturen von bis zu 111 Grad Celsius. Das System saß auf einem beweglichen Aufbau und wurde dem Sonnenstand nachgeführt.
Die Werte sind noch nicht optimal. Mit den Stromerträgen klassischer Fotovoltaik beispielsweise kann das System nicht konkurrieren. Als Nächstes wollen die Forschenden daher unter anderem die optischen Komponenten zur Lichtführung, das Wärmemanagement und die Solarzellen noch verbessern.

articles.title: Amazon makes its AI-powered Alexa+ free on Fire TV, no Prime required | TechCrunch
articles.text:
AI is coming to your TV, whether you want it or not.
On Wednesday, Amazon said its AI assistant, Alexa+, will be rolled out to all compatible Fire TV devices in the U.S. for free, whether or not the customer has a Prime subscription. The update brings conversational search, smart home controls, and AI-powered recommendations, the company says.
Previously, Alexa+ cost $19.99 per month for anyone who didn’t have an Amazon Prime membership, and was initially made available to the new Fire TV devices the company announced last fall.
Now, Amazon says that everyone will be upgraded to Alexa+ automatically. They won’t need to download an app or sign up for a subscription. Compatible devices include all the current-generation Amazon Fire TV Sticks, the Fire TV Cube, Amazon Ember smart TVs, and other smart TVs that have Alexa+ built in, including Hisense and Panasonic.
The move follows an industrywide push to make AI services available on more consumer electronic devices, often through non-optional upgrades like this. Google, for instance, rolled out Gemini to its Google TV platform earlier this year, replacing simple search features with AI-powered conversational modes. Roku upgraded its voice assistant to AI last year, too.
The companies point to metrics like time spent with the features to suggest positive consumer adoption trends. For instance, Amazon says that Alexa+ customers now have nearly twice as many conversations on Fire TV as they did with the original Alexa, which apparently suggests that customers with Alexa+ are no longer using their TV only as a lean-back source of entertainment, and are instead engaging with the AI, too.
Whether or not that’s a good thing is debatable.
Amazon says that with Alexa+, users don’t have to ask for shows by title, but can instead ask for suggestions based on other factors such as theme, age, or popularity — for example, “a top-rated thriller” or “a historical drama with a strong female lead.”
The AI bot can also help customers manage and control their smart home, including displaying their Ring camera feeds on the TV.

articles.title: ¡Ya es oficial! Venom se cruzará con Spider-Man en el Universo Marvel… aunque no como esperas
articles.text:
Desde que Spider-Man debutase en el Universo Cinematográfico de Marvel hace toda una década con Capitán América: Civil War, los fans esperan con ansias la llegada de Venom a su vida. Por suerte, estamos más cerca que nunca de verlo. Y es que el arácnido vivirá al fin su arco del simbionte en el próximo estreno que el UCM le tiene preparado. Eso sí, no es el que muchos esperarían.
Ya en Spider-Man: Brand New Day muchos esperaban ver a Venom. Se rumoreó que el personaje interpretado por Tom Hardy daría el salto definitivamente al UCM. De hecho, en el estudio tenían toda una narrativa planificada. Primero, ambos serían enemigos. Pero después unirían fuerzas para hacer frente a una amenaza mucho más temible, Knull, el dios de los simbiontes, que ya debutó brevemente en Venom 3. Finalmente, sin embargo, Sony y Marvel descartaron toda la idea para no seguir ampliando el caos multiversal.
En cualquier caso, ante los cambios físicos en Peter Parker que se anticipan en los tráileres de Spider-Man: Brand New Day, muchos fans seguían viendo al simbionte como una posibilidad real en la película. Pero tampoco fue así. Por ello, ahora las miradas están en la siguiente entrega. Pero aunque sabemos que Marvel y Sony Pictures ya trabajan en Spider-Man 5, en realidad Venom y Peter Parker se cruzarán antes en el Universo Cinematográfico de Marvel.
El debut de Venom en el UCM
Concretamente, Marvel ha hecho oficial que Venom debutará en su UCM en la serie Tu amigo y vecino Spider-Man. El título se estrenó en 2025 y recibió muy buenas críticas tanto de profesionales como de fans. Ahora, su segunda temporada está muy cerca, pues se estrenará en enero de 2027.
Y tal y como se ha confirmado en la convención D23, Venom será una parte fundamental de la temporada 2 de Tu amigo y vecino Spider-Man. En el evento, los fans pudieron ver un adelanto de lo que está por venir. En él, se pudo ver a Spider-Man enfrentándose a diferentes villanos como el Lagarto y Rhino. También se incluyó el debut de Gwen Stacy. Y Daredevil regresó en un nuevo cameo, como pasara en la teporada 1. Pero lo más interesante es que se enseñó cómo Spider-Man y Venom comienzan a forjar su vínculo.
Para quienes no la hayan visto, Tu amigo y vecino Spider-Man es una puerta de entrada muy interesante al superhéroe. Se trata de una variante alternativa a la de Tom Holland, por lo que forma parte del UCM pero en otra dimensión independiente. Así, hay numerosos cambios. Por ejemplo, se descubre cómo Peter obtuvo sus poderes por la picadura de una araña como consecuencia de una brutal pelea entre Doctor Strange y un peligroso simbionte.
Además, el mentor de Peter no es Tony Stark sino Norman Osborn, que en el futuro acabará convertido en el Duende Verde. Por su parte, Harry Osborn es amigo de Peter y también un influencer. En definitiva, cambios sustanciales que la convierten en una historia diferente y única. El escenario perfecto para la llegada de Venom en la temporada 2.

articles.title: Amazon’s Prime Air is taking off in nearly 500 US cities | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Amazon announced Wednesday a major expansion of Amazon Prime Air, its drone delivery service, with plans to reach nearly 500 U.S. cities by the end of 2026. This marks a significant milestone as it expands the service’s footprint by roughly 6x its current reach.
Prime Air will soon launch in 11 locations: Tolleson, Arizona; Ruskin, Florida; Kansas City, Kansas; Papillion, Nebraska; Baton Rouge, Louisiana; Hazel Park and Pontiac, Michigan; and Richmond, San Antonio, Richardson, and Waco, Texas.
The return to Tolleson is particularly notable given a drone accident that occurred there last year. In October 2025, two drones collided with the boom of a crane. Amazon’s drones have also previously drawn scrutiny following incidents, including clipping an internet cable and crashing into a garden and an apartment building.
This is likely why Amazon reiterated its focus on safety as part of the announcement. The company highlighted Prime Air’s “industry-leading Detect-and-Avoid system,” which is designed to continuously monitor the airspace and surroundings of each drone. The drones also rely on onboard cameras and sensors for navigation, obstacle detection, and delivery. Plus, Amazon said the drones are designed to operate in real-world conditions, including light rain and a range of temperatures.
Additionally, Prime Air operates under Federal Aviation Administration Part 135 certification, the same regulatory framework used by commercial air carriers.
“Customers already turn to Amazon for fast Same- and Next-Day Delivery, and Prime Air provides them an even speedier option when they need it, with deliveries in as fast as 30 minutes,” David Carbon, vice president of Amazon Prime Air, said in a statement, adding that the service has “already delivered hundreds of thousands of packages to customers by drone this year.”
The service currently operates across seven states, including Arizona, Florida, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Nebraska, and Texas. Amazon says launches in Georgia, Ohio, Illinois, Idaho, and New York are also coming soon.
Prime members receive free ultrafast drone delivery on eligible orders of $50 or more. For Prime members placing eligible orders under $50, the delivery fee is $2.99. Non-Prime customers pay a $4.99 delivery fee. Nearly all items 5 pounds or less can be delivered by drone.
Amazon’s push comes as other major companies continue building their own drone delivery networks. Walmart and Google parent Alphabet’s Wing have been expanding a competing drone delivery operation, which the companies have described as the largest drone delivery network in the U.S. In June, the companies added seven new markets, including Phoenix, Philadelphia, and the Bay Area.

articles.title: Il va falloir y retourner... Que s'est-il passé pendant la sortie spatiale de Sophie Adenot ?
articles.text:
Elle affiche un grand sourire en rentrant enfin à bord de la Station spatiale internationale (ISS). Sophie Adenot vient de passer 6 heures et 23 minutes dans l’espace, aux côtés de son collègue de la Nasa, Anil Menon, et devient ainsi la première femme française à avoir pu vivre cette expérience.
Durant cette sortie, leur emploi du temps était millimétré, avec une longue liste de tâches à accomplir, ce qui implique que le moindre grain de sable dans l’engrenage peut remettre en cause le planning de la sortie, ou causer un retard impossible à rattraper.
Des boulons récalcitrants après 4 heures de sortie
Comme il s’agissait de la toute première sortie de Sophie Adenot, elle avait droit à un petit moment pour contempler et appréhender ce tout nouvel environnement dans le vide spatial, et pour procéder aux vérifications de sécurité. Cinq minutes durant lesquelles elle devait donc contrôler son scaphandre et s’habituer à son environnement pendant qu’Anil Menon, qui pratiquait ici sa deuxième sortie, commençait les premières opérations.
Une fois ce délai passé, la mission démarrait avec le retrait de l’antenne défectueuse. Les deux astronautes ont commencé à débrancher les câbles, sans difficulté, mais ils ont ensuite dû s’attaquer aux boulons, et c’est là que les choses se sont compliquées.
Sophie Adenot et Anil Menon se sont chacun retrouvés face à des boulons récalcitrants environ quatre heures après le début de leur sortie. Ils en avaient quatre à retirer au total, et il leur a fallu beaucoup plus de temps que prévu pour en venir à bout.
Encore du travail pour la prochaine fois
Le scénario était le suivant : ils devaient retirer la vieille antenne, la mettre de côté, puis aller chercher la nouvelle qui était déjà fixée quelque part à l’extérieur de la station depuis une quinzaine d’années, et la mettre en place. Mais comme il a été très difficile de venir à bout des boulons de l’ancienne antenne, la Nasa a remis à jour le planning.
Finalement, l’antenne a bien été retirée, mais il était trop tard pour faire quoi que ce soit de plus. Les réserves des scaphandres (oxygène, batterie) étant limitées, il est impossible de laisser les astronautes sortir plus longtemps — outre le fait que c’est un exercice éprouvant physiquement et mentalement. Ils ont donc attaché provisoirement la vieille antenne à la structure de la Station, et n’ont pas touché à la nouvelle. Ce sera à d’autres astronautes, plus tard, de finir le travail.
Du point de vue de Sophie Adenot, la mission a tout de même été une réussite, car les difficultés qu’elle a rencontrées n’étaient pas de son fait. On ignore encore si elle devra à nouveau sortir avant la fin de son séjour dans l’ISS. Une autre sortie est prévue la semaine suivante, mais la participation de la Française n’a pas encore été confirmée. De plus, il s’agissait d’une autre opération différente de celle qui impliquait l’antenne défaillante, donc il est possible que le planning soit modifié.

articles.title: Running Local LLMs on the Arduino® UNO™ Q Board - EE Times
articles.text:
When talking about large language models (LLMs), people usually imagine a general-purpose assistant: something that can answer questions about weather, politics, software, history, travel, cooking, electronics – and almost any other topic. The model is expected to know a little bit about everything, follow open-ended conversations, and respond to a very broad range of prompts. That’s the experience most of us are used to, since cloud-based AI tools have become so widespread.
Embedded systems work in a much more “narrow” world. A robot does not need to discuss politics, an inspection system does not need to suggest vacation destinations, and a maintenance assistant installed near a machine does not need to explain ancient history. The system needs to understand the device, the task, the possible commands, the local data, and the actions that are safe to suggest or execute. The goal is to give an edge device enough language intelligence to become more useful, more understandable, and more independent from the network.
This is the framework in which we can think about local LLMs on UNO Q: a practical platform to explore this idea because it brings together a Debian Linux environment and the Arduino® hardware ecosystem. The Linux side can run local AI tools, command-line workflows, Python applications, web services, and inference runtimes. The Arduino side connects that intelligence to sensors, actuators, shields, Arduino® Modulino™ nodes, and real-world signals. This combination makes it possible to experiment with language models not as isolated chatbots, but as part of real embedded workflows.
The most important question to consider is not how to force a large model to run, but what kind of useful intelligence can live close to the data, close to the device, and close to the physical action?
Step 1: choose the right model for your use case
The edge is where smaller, optimized models become interesting. On the cloud, a large general-purpose model makes sense because it is expected to answer almost anything. On the edge, a model that has been trained, fine-tuned, distilled, or quantized for a specific domain can be more practical. It carries less unnecessary weight, focuses on the type of language the device actually needs, and can be integrated into a controlled application flow.
For example, in robotics the interaction can often be reduced to a limited set of useful instructions: move forward, stop, inspect this object, return to base, report battery level, explain the last error, switch to manual mode. The model can help interpret natural language, but the system should still map that interpretation to a controlled set of valid commands. This makes the behavior easier to test, easier to validate, and easier to trust.
That narrower scope is one of the reasons local LLMs can make sense on embedded platforms.
Step 2: understand your memory and storage constraints
A large language model usually has many parameters, and every parameter represents data that must be stored, loaded, and processed during inference. Model weights are only part of the story. During generation, the runtime also needs working memory for the prompt, the intermediate computation, and the key-value cache used by transformer models to keep track of previous tokens. As the context grows, memory usage grows too.
A 1B-parameter model in 4-bit quantization (such as Llama 3.2 1B Q4) occupies roughly 600–700 MB on disk and requires around 1 GB of RAM at runtime, including the KV cache for a short context window. A 3B model at the same precision pushes past 2 GB. These are numbers that matter on a board with fixed memory and storage, where the model must coexist with the OS, the runtime, and the rest of the application.
Quantization is one of the techniques that makes this more realistic. Instead of storing model weights with high-precision numerical values, a quantized model uses lower-precision representations. This reduces memory usage and can make inference possible on hardware that would otherwise be too constrained. In practical terms, quantization helps move a model from “too large to run locally” towards “small enough to experiment with” – while accepting a trade-off in accuracy, fluency, or speed depending on the model and runtime.
Model distillation is another important concept. In simple terms, distillation is a training approach where a smaller model learns from a larger teacher model. The goal is to keep useful behavior while reducing inference cost and memory footprint. A distilled model will not have the full breadth of the teacher, but it can be much more suitable when the application needs a focused capability on-device.
This example of running local LLMs and VLMs on UNO Q with yzma expands the conversation beyond text chat and explores local LLM and VLM workflows using yzma and llama, pointing toward a wider class of edge AI experiments where language models can work together with images, local data, and device context.
Step 3: identify where a local LLM adds real value
Local LLMs become even more useful when they are combined with other edge workflows. OCR is a good example. A camera connected to an UNO Q may extract text from a label, display, document, or machine interface. A compact language model can then summarize that text, classify it, or turn it into a structured response. The model only needs to process the relevant context, which keeps the workflow lighter and more focused.
The same principle applies to an UNO Q that collects logs, sensor readings, error states, or system events. A local model can turn that information into a short human-readable summary directly on the device. For a technician, this can transform raw data into something immediately useful – a compact explanation of the current status or a short description of the last error condition.
Step 4: design the architecture and set your boundaries
One of the most practical ways to think about local LLMs on UNO Q is to treat the model as an occasional reasoning layer. It can be called when language understanding, summarization, or interpretation adds value. Fast control loops, continuous monitoring, and timing-critical actions remain better suited to deterministic software running on the appropriate side of the system.
When working with local LLMs on UNO Q, developers should take into consideration a few practical parameters. Memory usage comes first: the model must fit comfortably together with the runtime and the rest of the application. Response latency comes next: a model that runs may still feel too slow if the use case expects instant answers. Storage should also be planned carefully, because model files and dependencies can be large.
The best entry point is the Arduino Project Hub tutorial Local LLM AI Chatbot on UNO Q, which walks through installing a small LLM and running it offline. It is a useful starting point because it demonstrates the basic shape of a local LLM application
There is also a natural bridge toward local agents. Agentic workflows can move beyond a simple chat interface and start coordinating tools, files, scripts, and actions. On UNO Q, this direction is especially interesting when the agent is treated as an orchestrator on the Linux side. It can inspect logs, prepare files, call scripts, interact with local tools, or help drive development workflows, while the hardware-facing layer keeps direct control over physical I/O.
This kind of setup requires clear boundaries. Giving an agent access to tools means giving it the ability to change things, so the environment should be designed carefully. A dedicated board can be a useful sandbox for this type of experimentation, with limited credentials, limited data access, and a specific set of allowed tools. This makes it possible to explore agentic workflows while keeping the system understandable and controlled.
If you prefer a familiar developer workflow, Installing Ollama on Arduino UNO Q covers a practical detail that matters a lot on embedded Linux systems: how to efficiently manage the resources available on the UNO Q to get the most out of it.
Step 5: run it, measure it, iterate
Pick one model, run it on the board, and pay attention to memory usage and response time for your specific prompt. That real-world data will tell you more than any benchmark – and it will give you a much clearer picture of where a local LLM fits in your next embedded project.
Local LLMs on UNO Q always balance power, cost, size, latency, privacy, reliability, and connectivity. The most interesting question is how much useful intelligence can be placed close to the data, the hardware, and the user. Because edge AI is not about more power. It’s about smarter choices. With the right model, the right architecture, and the flexibility of UNO Q, you can test local AI where it matters most: on real hardware, in real projects.
This video demonstrates how you can deploy lightweight LLMs on the Arduino UNO Q, opening the door to a new generation of intelligent, private, and responsive devices.
Start building with UNO Q and bring your AI ideas closer to the real world.

articles.title: Fairphone 6+ : le smartphone réparable passe à 12 Go de RAM et augmente son prix
articles.text:
Plus de RAM, une nouvelle puce et un nouveau coloris : voici ce qui change (et ce qui ne change pas) sur le nouveau smartphone réparable de Fairphone.
Le Fairphone 6+ est désormais officiel. Le constructeur néerlandais dévoile une version améliorée de son smartphone réparable, qui gagne en mémoire vive, adopte une puce plus récente et se décline dans un nouveau coloris Cobalt Blue, aux côtés des Forest Green et Horizon Black. Pour le reste, la fiche technique reste identique à celle du modèle précédent. Disponible dès maintenant sur le site officiel de la marque, le Fairphone 6+ est proposé à 649 euros sur le Vieux Continent.
Le Fairphone 6+ mise sur un nouveau processeur et plus de RAM
Sous le capot, le Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 prend la place de son prédécesseur, épaulé par 12 Go de RAM contre 8 Go pour le Fairphone 6. L'écran LTPO OLED de 6,31 pouces conserve sa définition de 1 116 x 2 484 pixels et son taux de rafraîchissement adaptatif jusqu'à 120 Hz. La batterie de 4 415 mAh reste compatible avec la charge rapide à 30 W.
La configuration photo ne bouge pas non plus. Le capteur principal de 50 mégapixels s'appuie sur le Sony Lytia 700C avec stabilisation optique et une ouverture à f/1,88. Un ultrawide de 13 mégapixels à f/2,2 et un objectif frontal de 32 mégapixels à f/2,0 complètent le trio. Le smartphone embarque Android 16, avec six mises à jour majeures garanties et des correctifs de sécurité promis jusqu'en 2032 ou 2033.
Une première commercialisation directe aux États-Unis
Sans surprise, la réparabilité demeure le principal argument de Fairphone. Le 6+ embarque ainsi 12 pièces remplaçables par l’utilisateur, dont la batterie, le port USB-C, l’écran et la coque arrière. Ces quatre éléments peuvent être changés en moins de cinq minutes à l’aide d’un seul tournevis. Les microphones, les boutons latéraux et le lecteur d’empreinte digitale nécessitent en revanche un passage par un centre de réparation. Fairphone prévoit par ailleurs de commercialiser les pièces détachées jusqu’en 2033 et accompagne son smartphone d’une garantie de cinq ans.
Pour la première fois, la marque commercialise directement aux États-Unis un smartphone fonctionnant avec une version standard d’Android, sans modification du système. Jusqu’ici, la marque s’appuyait notamment sur un partenariat avec e/OS pour proposer outre-Atlantique des versions dégooglisées de ses appareils.
Fairphone indique avoir réduit l’empreinte carbone liée à sa fabrication à 30 kg de CO₂e par appareil. Côté accessoires, la coque amovible permet d’ajouter séparément une dragonne, un anneau pour les doigts ou encore un porte-carte. Enfin, le Fairphone 6+ est commercialisé depuis ce mardi 18 août au prix de 649 euros.

articles.title: SA HR startup Jem raises $8.4m Series A funding round to support product expansion - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African startup Jem HR, a WhatsApp-based HR and employee benefits platform used by over 200 companies and 250,000 frontline workers, has raised a US$8.4 million Series A funding round to support its expansion into a workforce management platform.
Founded in 2019 as SmartWage, and rebranded in 2022, Jem HR started off by allowing companies to provide their employees with instant access to a percentage of their salaries and wages for work they have already done.
It then expanded beyond that, giving enterprises a simple yet effective way to digitise their most time-consuming HR processes, helping them save time and money in order to focus on people. The product gives employees without email the ability to receive company-wide communication, access their payslips, request leave and get access to financial wellness products, all via WhatsApp.
Jem, which raised a US43.3 million pre-Series A round last year, now plans further product expansion after raising a US$8.4 million Series A round, led by Quona Capital, which will support its expansion into a workforce management platform with new products such as time-and-attendance, credit scores and EAP already in place. Products like rostering, LMS, and more, are in beta.
“Jem is the workforce management platform for deskless employees,” said Jem co-founder and CEO Simon Ellis. “Employers have spent years stitching together a dozen disparate systems to run their teams. Jem is now the one place they can do all of it.”
Other investors include the University Technology Fund, E4E, Next176/FutureGrowth, and a group of prominent angel investors, including former Old Mutual CEO Iain Williamson.
“We backed Jem because it sits at a powerful intersection – essential workforce software that lets companies build a deeper relationship with their people, trusted employer distribution, and embedded financial services that save everyday South Africans meaningful amounts,” said Johan Bosini, venture partner at Quona Capital.
“Its WhatsApp-based platform is becoming an important infrastructure through which employers communicate with, manage and support their workforces.”

articles.title: How our perception of pain shapes our response to life
articles.text:
How our perception of pain shapes our response to life
Our suffering is often shaped by how we interpret difficult situations. Learn how changing your perspective can reduce emotional pain.
Life constantly presents situations we cannot control. Someone may criticise us, plans may fail, a person may disappoint us, or circumstances may suddenly change. While the event itself can be difficult, the way we interpret it often determines how deeply it affects us.
The Stoic philosopher Marcus Aurelius expressed this idea in the words, “If you are distressed by anything external, the pain is not due to the thing itself, but to your estimate of it.” His observation does not mean that difficult experiences are imaginary or that pain is always a choice. Rather, it encourages us to examine the meaning we attach to what happens.
The same event can affect people differently
Two people can experience the same situation and respond in completely different ways. One person may see criticism as an insult and spend the entire day thinking about it. Another may see the criticism as useful feedback and move forward without carrying the same emotional weight.
The external event has not changed. What has changed is the interpretation. Our beliefs, expectations and previous experiences influence the meaning we give to situations. This is why understanding our own thoughts can be just as important as understanding what happened.
Our thoughts can make problems feel bigger
A small disappointment can sometimes become overwhelming because of the story we create around it. A missed opportunity may turn into the belief that we will never succeed. Someone's silence may become evidence that they no longer care. One mistake may become proof that we are incapable.
The original event may be limited, but our interpretation can make it feel much larger. When we repeatedly think about the situation, imagine negative outcomes and attach personal meaning to it, emotional distress can increase.
Expectations influence how we experience life
Much of our frustration comes from the gap between what we expect and what actually happens. We expect people to behave a certain way, plans to work perfectly and life to follow the path we imagined. When reality refuses to cooperate, disappointment follows.
Expectations are not inherently wrong. They help us make plans and work towards goals. However, becoming too attached to a particular outcome can make ordinary setbacks feel like personal failures. Learning to accept that reality may differ from our expectations can make difficult situations easier to handle.
We cannot control everything outside us
One of the most practical lessons from Stoic philosophy is the distinction between what we can control and what we cannot. We cannot completely control another person's opinion, behaviour or decisions. We cannot control every unexpected event or guarantee a particular outcome.
What we can influence is our response. We can choose whether to react immediately or pause, whether to keep replaying an insult or let it go, and whether to focus on what went wrong or consider what we can do next. This shift in focus can create a greater sense of control.
Changing perspective does not mean ignoring pain
It is important not to misunderstand this idea. Changing our perspective does not mean pretending that painful experiences do not hurt. Loss, rejection, failure and betrayal can cause genuine emotional pain. Telling someone simply to “think positively” can sometimes dismiss what they are going through.
The deeper lesson is to acknowledge the pain while examining the thoughts surrounding it. Instead of asking why this happened to me or assuming the worst possible outcome, we can ask what is actually within my control and what meaning am I giving this situation.
Pause before reacting
Our first emotional reaction is not always our most thoughtful response. When something upsetting happens, we may immediately become angry, defensive or fearful. Acting from that first reaction can sometimes make the situation worse.
Creating a small pause gives the mind an opportunity to examine what happened. Asking ourselves what we know for certain, what we are assuming and whether there is another way to interpret the situation can prevent unnecessary suffering.
Perspective can turn setbacks into lessons
A setback does not have to be viewed only as something that went wrong. It can also become an opportunity to learn. A rejected application may encourage someone to improve their skills. A failed project may reveal weaknesses in their approach. A difficult conversation may teach them something about communication.
The situation itself may remain disappointing, but its meaning can change. Instead of seeing the experience only as evidence of failure, we can see it as information that helps us make better decisions in the future.
Freedom begins with understanding our response
We cannot build a life where nothing upsetting ever happens. People will disappoint us, plans will change and unexpected problems will appear. Waiting for perfect circumstances before allowing ourselves to feel peaceful can keep us trapped in constant frustration.
A more realistic goal is to develop greater control over our responses. When we understand that our interpretation influences our emotional experience, we gain an opportunity to question thoughts that automatically increase our suffering.
Learning to see things differently
Marcus Aurelius's observation remains relevant because it challenges us to look beyond the surface of difficult experiences. The external world will not always behave according to our wishes, but our relationship with what happens can change.
Sometimes the most powerful question is not, “Why did this happen to me?” but, “How am I choosing to understand what happened?” That question does not erase the difficulty, but it can prevent the difficulty from controlling the rest of our lives.
Our circumstances may be outside our complete control, but the meaning we give them deserves our attention. And sometimes, changing that meaning is the first step towards changing how we experience the pain.

articles.title: US charges Iranian hackers over $3.4 billion intellectual property theft
articles.text:
The U.S. has charged 17 Iranians, alleged members of a hacking-for-hire company called Mabna Institute, involved in years-long operations that stole data from American organizations.
Nine of the defendants were previously charged in a March 2018 indictment for hacking more than 300 universities and private companies.
The U.S. Justice Department (DoJ) has also announced rewards of up to $10 million for information leading to the location of five of the 17 Iranian defendants.
According to the U.S. government, the newly charged eight individuals stole academic research, intellectual property, emails, and other proprietary information.
The DoJ says that the Iranians listed below were involved in cyber operations for the Islamic Republic of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), other Iranian government bodies, universities, and paying customers.
- Saeid Houshyar
- Behzad Mesri, aka “Skote Vahshat”
- Manouchehr Hashemloo
- Keyvan Fayaz, aka “Achilles,” “The Joker,” and “bc.monster”
- Amir Barati
- Saber Shahbazi Ballojeh
- Arman Kahzadian
- Mojtaba Galekuhi, aka “Mojtaba Ghaleh Koui”
“Today’s charges, which include eight additional defendants, reveal the broader network allegedly behind a sweeping, state-sponsored campaign to steal research and intellectual property from American universities, businesses, and government institutions,” stated U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald.
“More than eight years after making the original indictment public, these charges make clear that the passage of time will not deter us from identifying and pursuing those who target the United States from abroad.”
The DoJ's announcement says the operation is believed to have begun around 2013 and targeted the accounts of more than 100,000 professors worldwide, successfully compromising roughly 8,000 of them.
Using access to these accounts, the hackers reportedly stole 31.5 terabytes of academic data, including journals, theses, dissertations, ebooks, and research across numerous disciplines, valued at approximately $3.4 billion.
This activity has impacted 178 universities, 144 of which are in the U.S., at least 53 private firms, 42 of which are in the U.S., two NGOs, and at least 10 U.S. state agencies.
One of the victims highlighted in the announcement was HBO, which was reportedly extorted for $6 million worth of Bitcoin.
The defendants now face charges related to conspiracy to commit computer intrusions, wire fraud, unauthorized access for financial gain, and aggravated identity theft, which can incur maximum penalties of up to 20 years in prison.
The State Department has also announced it is offering rewards of up to $10,000,000 for information leading to the whereabouts of Behzad Mesri, Mojtaba Galekuhi, Arman Kahzadian, Keyvan Fayaz, and Saber Shahbazi Ballojeh.
A Tor link has also been provided to allow anonymous submissions. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

articles.title: 5 Signs Your Customer Database Is Costing You Sales (and How to Fix It) - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Most businesses treat their customer or prospect database as a set and forget asset, built up once, added to occasionally, and rarely audited for quality. Database quality can decline gradually and often goes unnoticed. Peoplechange jobs, phone numbers get reassigned, email addresses become inactive and customers move.
By the time the declining contact rates or campaign performance reveal the problem, outdated data may have already been affecting results for months.
Signs Your Database Needs Attention
| Sign | What It Looks Like | Why It Matters | 
| Declining open and response rates | Fewer replies even though messaging has not changed | Unreachable contacts cannot respond, no matter how good the offer is | 
| Rising bounce rates | More emails failing to deliver over time | Can damage sender reputation, hurting delivery for quality contacts | 
| Wrong-person complaints | Replies like “this isn’t my number anymore” | Every one is a wasted outreach attempt and a possible compliance issue | 
| Manual data cleaning before every campaign | Staff scrubbing spreadsheets before launch | A recurring, often unaccounted for cost in staff time | 
| No review of data source in over a year | No memory of when the list was last validated | Databases should be audited and cleaned every twelve months to maintain quality | 
Declining Response Rates
If email open rates, call connect rates, or response rates have been trending down over recent campaigns, even though your offer and messaging have not fundamentally changed, stale data is one of the most common explanations. A campaign is only efficient if it can reach the right people at the right time.
Rising Bounce Rates
A rising bounce rate is one of the clearest technical signs of declining database quality. Beyond the immediate lost opportunity, high bounce rates can damage your sender reputation with email providers, making it harder for even your good contacts to receive future campaigns.
Complaints About Contacting the Wrong Person
If your team is fielding responses about wrong numbers or people who no longer work somewhere, that is not a one off annoyance, it is a symptom of a database that has not been validated in a while. Check your outreach practices against the Australian Communications and Media Authority’s Do Not Call Register rules, to ensure registered numbers are excluded from your database to avoid compliance risk.
Manual Cleanup Before Every Campaign
If launching a campaign requires staff to manually scrub spreadsheets or cross-check old records, outdated data is already costing the business time. This kind of manual cleanup can become a significant recurring expense, but it is easily overlooked because the work is spread across multiple tasks rather than appearing as a clear business cost.
No Recent Review of Your Data Source
Even accurate databases can decline in quality over time. If you cannot remember the last time your database was validated, cleaned or refreshed against current records, it is reasonable to assume a significant portion of it is no longer reliable.
(Image: Optimised and verified databases. Credit: kupicoo/iStock)
How to Fix a Declining Database
The fix is not necessarily starting from scratch. In many cases, the most cost effective solution is:
- A proper data cleaning and validation pass on your existing database
- Removing unresponsive contacts and correcting outdated details
- Re-verifying deliverability before running further campaigns
- Deciding, once the existing database is clean, whether you also need to supplement it with fresh, verified records
This is a more cost-effective option than continuing to run campaigns against an unoptimised list and absorbing the lost conversions quietly, campaign after campaign.
Opt-in marketing data and database cleaning services can offer exactly this combination for Australian businesses, data cleaning to validate and refresh existing databases, alongside access to contact records that are regularly checked and updated against current registers. For businesses that suspect their database may be negatively affecting campaign performance, validation and refresh is often the best option available, because every other part of your marketing, creative, targeting, offer, only performs as well as the data it is being sent to.
The Hidden Cost of Doing Nothing
An outdated database can reduce campaign performance while still consuming the same budget, staff time and creative resources. When this happens across multiple campaigns, the cost can quickly add up. Regular database cleaning and validation can help reduce this waste, while also limiting missed opportunities caused by incorrect or outdated contact details.

articles.title: Sous pression de l’Europe, Apple revoit les règles de l’App Store : voici tout ce qui change
articles.text:
L’Union européenne imposait à Apple de se plier au Digital Markets Act. L’entreprise à la pomme l’a fait. En effet, Apple a annoncé avoir établi, « en étroite collaboration avec la Commission européenne », de nouvelles règles imposées aux développeurs qui distribuent leurs applications sur les appareils Apple. Ainsi, la taxe Core Technology Fee est abandonnée, les paiements alternatifs deviennent plus accessibles et de nouvelles mesures sont instaurées pour protéger les plus jeunes. Si les développeurs peuvent signer ces nouvelles conditions dès aujourd’hui, ces changements entreront en vigueur le 1er octobre 2026.
Apple met fin à la taxe Core Technology Fee
Le principal changement concerne l’abandon de la taxe Core Technology Fee. Pour rappel, ce système imposait une taxe de 0,50 € appliquée à chaque première installation annuelle au-delà du premier million. Une application gratuite ou peu monétisée pouvait ainsi être soumise à cette taxe simplement parce qu’elle devenait soudainement virale. Apple a décidé de la supprimer pour la remplacer par une taxe baptisée Core Technology Commission de 5 %, appliquée à certaines transactions numériques réalisées dans les applications distribuées en dehors de l’App Store.
Les commissions de l’App Store vont également évoluer. Pour une application utilisant le système de paiement d’Apple, l’entreprise à la pomme prélèvera 26 %, ou 15 % pour les développeurs bénéficiant d’un taux réduit. Avec un système de paiement alternatif, la commission sera de 20 %, ou 10 % avec le taux réduit. Enfin, lorsqu’une application redirige l’utilisateur vers un site externe pour effectuer un paiement, Apple appliquera une commission de 15 %, ou de 10 % selon le cas.
Apple compte également simplifier l’utilisation des systèmes de paiement alternatifs. Les développeurs pourront notamment proposer le paiement d’Apple et une autre solution au sein d’une même application. Par ailleurs, Apple assouplit ses règles concernant la distribution des applications en dehors de l’App Store. Les développeurs pourront notamment passer par des boutiques alternatives ou distribuer leurs applications directement depuis le Web.
Des mesures pour protéger les plus jeunes
Apple met en place plusieurs mesures pour protéger les enfants lors des paiements alternatifs. Ainsi, les applications de la catégorie « Enfants » ne pourront pas contenir de liens permettant de se rendre sur un site externe pour effectuer un achat. Pour les moins de 18 ans, les applications qui utilisent un système de paiement alternatif ou redirigent vers un site Web devront afficher un contrôle parental. Ainsi, un parent ou un tuteur devra approuver un achat. Pour les moins de 13 ans, ces redirections vers des sites externes seront tout simplement interdites.
Ces nouvelles règles concernent avant tout les développeurs. Néanmoins, pour les utilisateurs, elles devraient permettre davantage de choix concernant les boutiques d’applications et les moyens de paiement.
