articles.title: London’s Medly raises €6.9 million to democratise access to personalised education through an AI tutor | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Medly AI, a London-based AI-powered learning platform that claims to offer the world’s first AI tutor for exam prep, has raised a €6.89 million ($8 million) Seed round.
The round was led by Felix Capital and backed by existing investors Eka Ventures and Ada Ventures. Several angel investors also participated in the round, including Andrey Dobrynin, CEO at InvestEngine; Al Giles, Venture Partner at Creator Fund; Jean Hammond, General Partner at LearnLaunch Accelerator; and Hector Mason, General Partner at Episode 1 Ventures.
Dr. Paul Jung, co-founder and CEO of Medly, commented, “Almost a third of 11–16-year-olds receive some form of private tutoring. For those who can afford it, it’s a powerful advantage. For those who can’t, it’s an equally powerful reinforcer of the status quo.
“We’ve built something to disrupt that. Our custom AI gives every child access to a 24/7 personal tutor that adapts to how they learn and responds to their unique needs. In just one exam season, the majority of students using Medly were able to improve by at least an entire grade – that’s a game-changer for young people. This capital will enable us to support even more students and prove that tailored academic help can come without a premium price tag.”
Medly was founded by UCL medicine graduates Dr. Paul Jung and Dr. Kavi Samra, who met during their first year of secondary school at age 11. They both left careers in the NHS to build Medly.
Since in-person private tutoring is typically quite expensive, Medly’s mission is to democratise education by providing a personalised AI tutor for every student. The company states that it offers on-demand academic support at a fraction of the cost, making it more accessible to students from all backgrounds.
According to Medly, as more students use generative AI tools such as ChatGPT to help with their studies, the platform provides purpose-built, accuracy-tested support rather than relying on the questionable insights of standard generative AI platforms.
The company highlights that its AI is based on neuroscience and teaching theory, and has been designed to act as a personal tutor for students. It mentions that the AI tutor is built on a proprietary combination of seven LLMs and can deliver a tailored service to each student, tracking progress, intuiting learning styles and leveraging teaching theory to tailor feedback style.
“Medly provides instant feedback on answers to practice questions and shares advice on where students could gain more marks – all through a bespoke conversational user interface. Additional AI features make study feel even more personalised. For example, handwriting recognition lets students write directly on the platform using tablets or styluses, and is the most natural mode of learning for subjects such as Maths and Chemistry,” the company mentioned in the press release.
Medly can be used by students preparing for their GCSE, IGCSE, A-Level and International Baccalaureate exams. It also has a curriculum-agnostic product called Medly Open, tailored for university students.
The company reported that, among students who used the platform to prepare for their GCSE exams last summer, 74% improved by at least one grade and 41% improved by two or more grades. It further notes that the biggest improvements were seen among those taking Physics and English Literature GCSEs, with grades jumping by 46% and 43%, respectively.
The capital will be used to grow the community of students Medly supports in the UK and roll-out support across additional international markets. In the US, Medly has recently launched SATs, showing promising early traction, and is iterating rapidly, with plans to expand to APs and ACTs by the end of this year.
It will also be used to expand Medly’s evidence base. The team recently published its first research paper, evidencing the platform’s marking performance compared to human examiners, and has just completed a randomised controlled trial with over 1,000 UK students to demonstrate its ability to increase grade attainment in lower-attaining schools.
The company also plans to enhance its capabilities and develop proprietary models for specific UK/EEA educational functions, such as marking and pedagogy. The platform is also introducing new features designed to push the most capable students beyond the regular exam curriculum, deepening their knowledge and preparing them for higher education.
Since launching in February 2025, the platform has scaled its user base by almost 600%, rapidly growing to over 400,000 users in the UK alone. It was also awarded the Department for Education’s competitive AI Tutoring Tools Pioneers Programme grant in July this year, which is focused on improving the academic attainment of disadvantaged pupils across England.

articles.title: IA, vídeos verticais e dados mudam experiência dos fãs na Copa do Mundo 2026
articles.text:
A forma de acompanhar uma Copa do Mundo está mudando. Além da transmissão tradicional, vídeos verticais, diferentes câmeras, estatísticas, enquetes e conteúdos personalizados começam a fazer parte da experiência dos torcedores.
O tema foi discutido no painel “A Nova Experiência do Fã na Copa do Mundo 2026: Imersão, Interatividade e Dados em Tempo Real”, realizado durante a SET Expo.
Vídeos verticais ganham espaço
O consumo de vídeos verticais cresceu durante a Copa do Mundo 2026. Segundo dados apresentados no painel, um único clipe publicado no TikTok chegou a 130 milhões de visualizações.
A inteligência artificial já permite transformar automaticamente imagens em 16:9 para 9:16. A tecnologia utiliza metadados para identificar a posição dos jogadores e determinar o ponto de foco do vídeo, inclusive durante transmissões ao vivo.
O formato também pode funcionar como uma segunda tela, levando o usuário de um conteúdo curto para a transmissão completa.
Dados ajudam torcedor a encontrar onde assistir
John Morash, da Gracenote, destacou outro problema: espectadores levam, em média, 14 minutos para encontrar uma partida, enquanto 60% ainda enfrentam dificuldades relacionadas à disponibilidade.
Uma das soluções apresentadas é o OnSports, que conecta diferentes transmissões, idiomas, canais e plataformas a um mesmo evento.
Os metadados também permitem recomendar conteúdos relacionados após a partida ou oferecer outras formas de acompanhar uma competição, como escolher a câmera de um piloto durante uma corrida de Fórmula 1.
IA cria interações durante as partidas
Tarik, da Rooster, mostrou como diferentes sinais podem ser processados por inteligência artificial para gerar enquetes, quizzes e estatísticas em tempo real.
Em um dos exemplos apresentados, uma enquete foi criada poucos segundos após um gol de Martinelli contra o Japão e registrou 98,9% de engajamento.
A tecnologia também permite publicidade contextual. Em vez de anúncios estáticos, marcas podem reagir aos acontecimentos da própria partida.
Transmissões podem ficar cada vez mais personalizadas
Até 2030, a tendência apresentada no painel é que diferentes espectadores possam receber conteúdos diferentes durante o mesmo evento.
Um usuário poderia receber vídeos verticais focados em seu jogador favorito, enquanto estatísticas, anúncios e interações seriam selecionados de acordo com seus interesses.
Ainda existem desafios, principalmente relacionados à latência e sincronização das transmissões, mas a evolução dos dados e da inteligência artificial aponta para uma experiência esportiva cada vez mais personalizada.
Nesse cenário, assistir a uma Copa do Mundo deixa de significar apenas receber uma transmissão igual para todos. O mesmo jogo poderá gerar experiências diferentes para cada torcedor.

articles.title: 'Linternas', la nueva serie de Linterna Verde, bate el récord histórico del Universo DC en Rotten Tomatoes
articles.text:
El Universo DC de James Gunn y Peter Safran acaba de estrenar una nueva serie en HBO Max y, a juzgar por las primeras reacciones, ha dado de lleno en el clavo. Y es que en apenas unas pocas horas ha batido uno de los récords más difíciles que podía. Se trata de Linternas, un proyecto centrado en los Linterna Verde. Pero, a diferencia de otros proyectos de la compañía, este título abraza por completo su lado más adulto y profundo con un thriller policiaco al estilo True Detective.
El embargo de las críticas profesionales se levantó un par de días antes del estreno de la serie en HBO Max y consiguió una puntuación extraordinaria de 91% en Rotten Tomatoes. Ya puedes leer nuestra crítica en este enlace. Esto la situaba por encima de películas como Superman (83%) y Supergirl (52%), aunque por debajo de series como Creature Commandos (93%) y la temporada 2 de Peacemaker (94%).
Sin embargo, en las últimas horas la situación ha dado un inesperado vuelco. A medida que más profesionales han publicado sus críticas, la puntuación de la serie ha crecido. Así, Linternas acaba de llegar a un 95% en Rotten Tomatoes, lo que la convierte en el proyecto mejor valorado de la historia del nuevo Universo DC. Además, entre la audiencia también es uno de los que mejor nota tiene con un 85%, únicamente por detrás del 90% de Superman. Queda claro que la serie de Linterna Verde es ya un éxito para la franquicia.
| Serie | Nota Rotten Tomatoes crítica | Nota Rotten Tomatoes audiencia | 
| Linternas | 95% | 85% | 
| Peacemaker temporada 2 | 94% | 79% | 
| Creature Commandos | 93% | 79% | 
| Superman | 83% | 90% | 
| Supergirl | 52% | 73% | 
De qué va Linternas
La serie nos presenta a Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) y John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), dos miembros del grupo de los Linterna Verde. El primero es toda una leyenda del cuerpo, pero el segundo es un nuevo recluta que lleva tan solo un par de meses entrenando y ni siquiera se ha ganado el anillo. Así, los dos policías intergalácticos se verán envueltos en un oscuro misterio en el planeta Tierra mientras investigan un asesinato en el corazón de Estados Unidos.
El reparto principal lo componen Kyle Chandler y Aaron Pierre. Junto a ellos, nombres de la talla de Laura Linney, Kelly Macdonald, Garret Dillahunt, Poorna Jagannathan, Jason Ritter, Ulrich Thomsen, Nathan Fillion, J. Alphonse Nicholson y Jasmine Cephas Jones. Por su parte, Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof y Tom King ejercen de cocreadores de Linternas.

articles.title: Einschlafen in 2 Minuten: Das taugt die Military Sleep Method wirklich
articles.text:
Einschlafen in 2 Minuten: Das taugt die Military Sleep Method wirklich
Die „Military Sleep Method“ erlebt derzeit eine Renaissance in sozialen Medien. Es handelt sich um eine Technik, die angeblich von der US-Armee entwickelt wurde, um Soldat:innen zu helfen, unter extremen Stressbedingungen – sogar im Sitzen und bei Lärm – innerhalb von zwei Minuten einzuschlafen.
Der Ursprung dieser Methode liegt jedoch nicht in einem geheimen Militärhandbuch, sondern in einem Sport-Ratgeber aus dem Jahr 1981. Lloyd „Bud“ Winter, ein US-amerikanischer Sprint-Trainer, beschrieb die Technik in seinem Buch „Relax and Win: Championship Performance“. Er soll sie für Pilot:innen der U.S. Navy Pre-Flight School im Zweiten Weltkrieg entwickelt haben.
Was die Methode verspricht
Die Methode selbst ist eine strukturierte Abfolge von Entspannungstechniken, die in etwa zwei Minuten durchgeführt werden soll.
Sie besteht im Kern aus drei Phasen: Zuerst eine Form der Progressiven Muskelentspannung, bei der das Gesicht, die Schultern, Arme und Beine systematisch entspannt werden. Zweitens wird die Atmung kontrolliert, wobei der Fokus auf einer langsamen, tiefen Ausatmung liegt. Drittens folgt eine Visualisierung, bei der sich die Anwender:innen eine ruhige Szene vorstellen sollen, etwa in einem Kanu auf einem stillen See zu liegen.
Die Wissenschaft hinter der Technik
Auf den ersten Blick wirkt dies plausibel. Eine direkte wissenschaftliche Validierung der „Military Sleep Method“ als Gesamtpaket oder der 2-Minuten-Behauptung existiert jedoch nicht. Es gibt keine modernen, von Fachleuten geprüften Studien, die diese spezifische Methode untersucht haben.
Was es aber gibt, ist eine Fülle von Belegen für die Wirksamkeit der einzelnen Komponenten. Wie Dean J. Miller, ein Schlafforscher an der CQUniversity Australia, in einem Beitrag für The Conversation analysiert, sind diese Techniken nahezu identisch mit jenen, die in der Kognitiven Verhaltenstherapie bei Insomnie (CBT-I) eingesetzt werden.
Die CBT-I gilt als wissenschaftlicher Goldstandard in der Behandlung von Schlafstörungen. Progressive Muskelentspannung und kontrollierte Atmung reduzieren nachweislich die körperliche Anspannung und helfen dem Nervensystem, in den Ruhemodus zu schalten.
Das unrealistische 2-Minuten-Ziel
Das eigentliche Problem der Methode ist nicht die Technik, sondern das Marketing-Versprechen der zwei Minuten. Für gesunde Erwachsene gilt eine Einschlafzeit (Schlaflatenz) von zehn bis 20 Minuten als völlig normal und gesund.
Experten wie Miller, aber auch die Cleveland Clinic, warnen davor, dass dieses 2-Minuten-Ziel für die meisten Zivilist:innen unrealistisch ist. Wer regelmäßig deutlich schneller einschläft – etwa in unter fünf Minuten – leidet möglicherweise nicht unter Einschlafproblemen, sondern unter starkem Schlafentzug.
Hier liegt auch der Unterschied zum militärischen Kontext: Soldat:innen im Einsatz oder Pilot:innen im Krieg leiden oft unter extremem Schlafmangel, wie die Sleep Foundation in Analysen zum Schlaf im Militär darlegt. Ein hoher Schlafdruck führt naturgemäß zu einer sehr kurzen Einschlaflatenz.
Die Gefahr des Leistungsdrucks
Für Anwender:innen, die abends entspannt im Bett liegen, kann die Fixierung auf die Stoppuhr sogar kontraproduktiv sein.
Wenn das Einschlafen nach 120 Sekunden nicht gelingt, entsteht schnell Frustration und Leistungsdruck. Genau diese Sorge, nicht einschlafen zu können, ist einer der stärksten Faktoren, die Menschen wach halten. Die Methode kann somit „nach hinten losgehen“, wie es die Cleveland Clinic formuliert.
Auch die oft zitierte Erfolgsquote von 96 Prozent ist mit Vorsicht zu genießen. Sie stammt nicht aus einer modernen Studie, sondern aus Winters ursprünglichem Bericht und bezog sich auf Pilot:innen, die die Methode sechs Wochen lang konsequent trainierten.
Fazit: Ein Werkzeug, kein Wundermittel
Die „Military Sleep Method“ ist kein magischer Schalter zum Einschlafen. Sie ist vielmehr nur ein Re-Branding von altbekannten und wissenschaftlich fundierten Entspannungstechniken.
Wer die Methode nutzen möchte, kann dies tun, sollte aber das 2-Minuten-Ziel ignorieren. Stellt euch die Technik nicht als Rennen gegen die Uhr vor, sondern als ein Ritual, um den Körper und den Geist auf die Nacht vorzubereiten. Die Entspannung ist das Ziel, nicht die Rekordzeit.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 22.10.2025 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.
Ich zähle von Hundert auf Eins in Einer-Schritten rückwärts und versuche mir die jeweilige Ziffer auch vorzustellen. Komme selten auf Eins
I tried it back when I was in the Army… but unfortunately, it didn’t work for me.
Sommerloch noch nicht zu Ende? Die Story kommt gefühlt jedes Jahr irgendwo wieder. Vermutlich seit 1981, wie es der Artikel angibt.

articles.title: The founder's secret weapon: Work at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 and learn how the pros do it | TechCrunch

Want to know what separates the founders and operators who build industry-defining companies from everyone else? They understand how ecosystems work. They’ve seen how the best events are orchestrated, how networks are built, and how real opportunities emerge.
You can get an insider’s view by volunteering at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, taking place October 13-15 at San Francisco’s Moscone West.

- How world-class tech events get built (logistics, crowd management, experience design).

The people running TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 learned by doing it. Now it’s your turn.

To volunteer, you need to:

We prefer volunteers to be local to San Francisco but it’s not required.
Apply before spots fill up
The best networkers in tech aren’t just attendees — they’re also part of the team that makes it happen. Become a TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 volunteer.

articles.title: OpenAI hit the brakes. Now what?
articles.text:
With a looming IPO, intense competition from Anthropic, and Chinese and open-weight rivals nipping at its heels, OpenAI has plenty of reasons to move fast. Instead, it hit the brakes.
OpenAI hit the brakes. Now what?
AI safety still depends largely on the industry policing itself.
On Tuesday, the company said it had slowed the pace of some AI development while it tightened security and safeguards. That included a two-week pause in reinforcement learning training on its “latest models intended for deployment,” and an ongoing delay to its “largest planned frontier RL run.”
The decision is a very public test of an idea AI safety advocates have pushed for for years: that companies should be willing to bow out of the AI race and slow things down when their safeguards fail to keep up with what they are building. But as the race around them continues, will slowing down accomplish anything?
“For the pause to be sustainable, it has to be made industry-wide.”
For all the talk of slowing down, OpenAI isn’t exactly standing still. The company said it is “pacing” development, a fuzzy and imprecise term that has nevertheless become part of the industry’s lexicon in recent months. In practice, the slowdown is narrowly scoped. OpenAI’s announcement says the pause only covers models meant for deployment while it beefs up security and monitoring before it runs the kind of tests where models may be capable of getting out and hacking real targets. It doesn’t necessarily mean there will be a significant slowdown of the company’s broader development.
There is, of course, a very good reason for OpenAI to focus on securing such systems before testing them. Just last month, OpenAI disclosed that its models broke out of a supposedly secure testing environment and hacked developer platform Hugging Face, without OpenAI noticing. The incident prompted a wider review of testing practices in the industry that uncovered similar episodes involving more models from OpenAI, as well as models from Anthropic and Meta. OpenAI has every reason to avoid a repeat, particularly with growing scrutiny from lawmakers.
From the outside, it’s hard to tell how sincere OpenAI is about stopping solely for the sake of safety, particularly when the company and senior staff have been so vocal about it. But the company’s commitment to safety has been called into question in recent months following a series of high-profile safety team departures and the disbanding of its preparedness team. OpenAI did not respond to The Verge’s request for comment.
There are good reasons to take OpenAI’s slowdown seriously. Experts who spoke to The Verge pointed to the costs of slowing down at a time of intense competition. Every delay gives rivals more time to catch up or extend their lead. “Due to the intensity of the AI race, everyone has an incentive to work at breakneck speed,” said Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and cofounder of Apollo Research, an AI safety research organization. “Voluntarily slowing down worsens your positioning in the race, so it’s not something that a lab would do lightly.”
The decision also broadly fits with OpenAI’s own published safety doctrine, its Preparedness Framework, as well as the safety frameworks of other AI companies, said Alan Chan, a research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI. “The basic principle is: Continue with development and/or deployment only when we have the mitigations that enable doing so with acceptable risk,” Chan said. As part of the new safety measures, OpenAI said it plans to review and “evolve” the framework — much of which dates back to 2023, when it was first published — to account for advances in its models.
There are also good reasons to believe the new safeguards will actually make OpenAI’s systems safer, at least in the short term, though experts cautioned that this is difficult to assess without more information. “These are good steps that, implemented well, are probably enough to prevent the current generation of agents from causing harm,” Adam Gleave, cofounder and CEO of AI safety organization FAR.AI, told The Verge. “The key question is how OpenAI will keep pace as capabilities increase.”
Gleave’s question points to a broader problem: If technical safeguards falter again, what then? Nothing required OpenAI to stop and take stock this time, which is what made its willingness to do so meaningful. But it also means there is nothing guaranteeing OpenAI — or any other AI company — will make the same choice next time.
“Pacing buys time, not safety… An effective pacing strategy cannot be improvised during a crisis.”
Relying on companies to make that call themselves is a precarious form of governance, particularly in an industry where, as Hobbhahn noted, there is every incentive to keep going. Nick Moës, executive director of nonprofit AI safety and governance organization The Future Society, described self-policing as the structural problem at the heart of the current approach to AI safety. He argued it should be possible for governments to decide whether OpenAI or any other company should pause development of a technology deemed unsafe. “This is how most industries operate,” he said, pointing to drugs, construction, aircraft, and even restaurants as sectors with stronger regulatory oversight than AI.
Voluntary measures also risk the industry converging on the lowest common denominator. If slowing down imposes a cost, companies have an incentive to adopt only the measures their rivals are also willing to accept. That pressure becomes particularly acute as the race tightens. If OpenAI repeatedly slows down development while its competitors do not, it “will simply be replaced by Anthropic,” Moës argued. “For the pause to be sustainable, it has to be made industry-wide.”
Sustainable safety needs something stronger than voluntary action. Moës said government oversight could fill that void, as it does in other industries. Independent verification could play a part too. Chan said making sure companies actually implement safety measures will be especially important as technical mitigations like monitoring AIs becomes more expensive. Hobbhahn concurred: “It’s always hard to tell from the outside if a lab is sincere about pausing or safety more broadly, so having more evidence and an independent party to validate the claim is super important.”
Even a perfectly transparent pause is only useful if something actually happens during it. “Pacing buys time, not safety,” said Brianna Rosen, research director for frontier security at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy. The point is to create breathing room for companies and governments to understand risks and respond appropriately. This would mean deciding what would trigger a slowdown — as well as what happens during one and conditions needed to end one — ahead of time. “An effective pacing strategy cannot be improvised during a crisis,” she said.
It’s possible OpenAI’s slowdown will set a precedent for the industry. Many of the experts The Verge spoke to hoped other companies would follow its lead, whether voluntary or because stronger rules eventually compel them to. But in an industry still largely policed by itself, there is little stopping its competitors — or OpenAI itself — from racing straight past that precedent next time safety and speed conflict.

articles.title: Tejaswini Hebalkar on breaking barriers; How Milkvilla is building a 12-hour supply chain for fresh milk
articles.text:
Tejaswini Hebalkar on breaking barriers; How Milkvilla is building a 12-hour supply chain for fresh milk
From engineering and consulting to leading digital transformation at Allstate, Tejaswini Hebalkar’s career has spanned technology, operations, and business. Meanwhile, Bengaluru-based dairytech startup Milkvilla operates a hyperlocal model that takes milk from farmer to customer in 12 hours.
Dear Reader,
India now has an AI foundation model built specifically for payments.
The country’s payments ecosystem is growing at an extraordinary scale, but this has created a complex environment. Fintech firm Razorpay hopes to address this with Vulcan, an AI model that promises to make online payments more reliable, secure, and successful.
Developed with NVIDIA and AWS, Vulcan has been trained on nearly 3 trillion data points across 4 billion payments. It aims to improve payment routing, fraud detection, and checkout experiences through a single AI system.
In other news, US-based startup Wispr has raised $280 million in a Series B funding round at a $2 billion valuation.
Wispr’s AI tools convert spoken language into written text, including emails, messages and documents. The newly-raised capital will be used to improve speech recognition accuracy, which Co-founder Tanay Kothari says, will determine whether voice tech becomes a genuine substitute for typing rather than remaining a novelty.
Meanwhile, Dharwad pedha is having its moment under the sun.
Dharwad Big Mishra Pedha, a 93-year-old confectionery maker from Karnataka, has raised Rs 300 crore from Bharat Value Fund of The Wealth Company to expand its network. Founded in 1933, the company has 200 outlets across North Karnataka, Goa, and Southern Maharashtra, selling GI-tagged Dharwad pedha and other sweets and snacks. The investment underscores the big opportunity in branded regional foods.
From sweet, steady success to rapid growth…
Ahead of its potential market listing later this year, Anthropic is in peak form. According to a source, the AI startup’s annual revenue run rate topped $65 billion by the end of July, soaring from $47 billion in May and $9 billion at the end of 2025. Anthropic is projecting a revenue of $190 billion to $200 billion in 2028.
In today’s newsletter, we will talk about
- Tejaswini Hebalkar on breaking barriers, embracing AI
- How Milkvilla is building a 12-hour supply chain for fresh milk
Here’s your trivia for today: Which pasta is shaped like a bicycle? (Scroll down for the answer)
Women in Tech
Tejaswini Hebalkar on breaking barriers, embracing AI
From engineering and consulting to leading digital transformation at Allstate, Tejaswini Hebalkar’s career has spanned technology, operations, and business. Now, as the SVP of Operations, she is focused on building a “human plus AI” workplace while championing women through the often-overlooked mid-career phase.
Key takeaways:
- Tejaswini’s career moved from engineering at Lucent Technologies to consulting and eventually digital transformation, where she built tech-enabled repair and supply-chain operations at SquareTrade before its acquisition by Allstate.
- She highlights the disproportionate drop-off of women at the mid-career stage and advocates for mentorship, sponsorship, and strong support networks to help women navigate career crossroads.
- As AI takes on more transactional and analytical work, Tejaswini believes empathy, relationships, and leadership will become even more important, and sees AI as an opportunity to democratise technical skills.
Funding Alert
Startup: NeoGeoInfo Technologies
Amount: $20M
Round: Series A
Startup: Rezolv
Amount: $12.5M
Round: Series A
In-focus
How Milkvilla is building a 12-hour supply chain for fresh milk
Bengaluru-based dairytech startup Milkvilla operates a hyperlocal model that takes milk from farmer to customer in 12 hours, while keeping 60-70% of revenue with its network of dairy farmers. The company has also expanded beyond milk and delivers products such as paneer, ghee and peda. These products follow the same supply chain, which Milkvilla had recently patented.
The logistics of it all:
- The company follows a hyperlocal procurement model, sourcing milk close to the cities where it operates. In Muzaffarpur, in Bihar, where founders Mannu Jee and Aman Jee come from, Milkvilla works with farmers in the neighbouring villages. In Bengaluru, the milk comes from dairy farmers in Ramanagara district, about 50 km southwest of the city.
- Milkvilla’s special milk collection vehicle is equipped with a cooling and a testing infrastructure. The vehicle goes to the farmer’s doorstep, and then the milk is turbo-cooled down to four degree Celsius. This increases the milk’s shelf life to 24 hours without the need for any chemicals.
- The milk is then taken to a delivery hub, where it undergoes quality assessment tests. Once it passes the required metrics, it is loaded into a refrigerated van for delivery to customers.
News & updates
- Acquisition: Wipro Consumer Care is on a shopping spree. After buying the Good Home and Eva brands from TTK Healthcare, and S Brands in the Philippines recently, the company has now acquired Ahmedabad-based premium beauty and skincare brand Dermatouch for Rs 387.5 crore.
- ChatGPT for Teens: OpenAI has launched a specialised version of its AI platform called ChatGPT for Teens. This initiative aims to provide younger users with a tool for critical thinking and learning while embedding significant safety measures to protect them from harmful content.
- Meta trial: US states have called for big changes to Instagram and Facebook as Meta child privacy trial begins. Not only are the states seeking upwards of $1 trillion from Meta, they are also demanding changes including ending ‘like’ counts and infinite scroll.

articles.title: Mehr Privatsphäre in Windows 11: Auf diese Änderungen warten manche Nutzer schon lange
articles.text:
Praktische Neuerung für Windows 11: Wie eine kleine Änderung dir mehr Privatsphäre geben soll
Wer mit einem Windows-Laptop arbeitet oder den Desktop-PC mit Peripherie ausgestattet hat, sollte auf seine Privatsphäre achten. Mikrofon und Webcam können im Grunde von jeder Anwendung angefragt und mit Erlaubnis genutzt werden. Wenn Apps diese Berechtigung ausnutzen, kann es zu Problemen kommen. Um dir mehr Kontrolle darüber zu geben, welche Apps und Dienste Zugriff bekommen dürfen, arbeitet Microsoft an einer Neuerung.
Windows 11: So bekommst du mehr Privatsphäre
Unter Windows 11 kannst du in den Einstellungen den Bereich „Datenschutz & Sicherheit“ aufrufen. Unter den App-Berechtigungen kannst du dann festlegen, welche Anwendungen auf dein Mikrofon, deine Webcam oder deinen Standort zugreifen dürfen. Bisher unterscheidet Microsoft dabei zwei App-Typen: solche, die aus dem Microsoft Store geladen wurden, und alle Apps, die über andere Wege auf dem Windows-PC gelandet sind.
Das Problem daran: Während die Store-Apps alle eigene Schieberegler bieten, um den Zugriff auf Mikrofon, Webcam und Standort separat zu regeln, werden alle anderen Anwendungen unter einem einzigen Schalter zusammengefasst. Wer also beispielsweise mehrere Browser, Discord und Zoom benutzt, kann nicht einzelnen Diensten den Zugriff gewähren und andere dafür ausschließen.
Wie Windows Latest berichtet, soll sich das aber mit einem künftigen Update für Windows 11 ändern. Schon jetzt testet Microsoft die Änderung im Experimental-Build des Betriebssystems. Sobald das Update installiert wurde, erhalten alle Anwendungen einen eigenen Schieberegler, um die Zugriffe separat zu steuern. Es ist nicht mehr relevant, ob sie aus dem Microsoft Store stammen oder von einer anderen Quelle geladen und installiert wurden.
Damit würde Microsoft Einstellungen ändern, die schon seit Windows 10 Version 1903 Teil des Betriebssystems sind. Das Update erschien im Mai 2019 für den Vorgänger von Windows 11. Ob die Änderung letztlich in der Release-Version von Windows 11 landet, bleibt abzuwarten. Der Experimental-Build ist für Tests von neuen Funktionen gedacht. Sollten sie große Probleme bereiten oder keinen wirklichen Nutzen mit sich bringen, kann Microsoft sie auch wieder aus Windows 11 entfernen.

articles.title: Multi Agent Collaboration Gets Persistent Compute in Bedrock AgentCore
articles.text:
Amazon Web Services has introduced runtime instances in the Bedrock AgentCore news blog, adding a second compute option that runs agents on managed Amazon EC2 in a customer account while keeping the existing AgentCore APIs, identity and observability model. The feature is aimed at teams whose agents no longer fit neatly into the eight hour microVM ceiling that AgentCore launched with, based on serverless microVM based sessions.
In the announcement, principal developer advocate Sebastien Stormacq explains that runtime instances give agents persistent EC2-backed sessions that can run for up to fourteen days, with shared file systems, GPU accelerated instance types, and support for Python and container images. Multiple agents can be deployed into a single runtime and collaborate on the same host through a shared session directory, rather than calling each others APIs for every handoff. Stormacq notes that teams can bring frameworks such as CrewAI, LangGraph, LlamaIndex and Strands without changing their packaging model, using a simple @app.entrypoint decorator and either a zip file or container image.
Runtime instances handles all of that for you while integrating with the same AgentCore APIs, identity controls, and observability you already use with AgentCore Runtime microVMs.
- Sebastien Stormacq
The blog post uses an example which illustrates the multi-agent collaboration pattern that runtime instances are designed to support, where several specialised agents operate over a common working directory for code, tests, documentation and security artefacts.
AWS positions runtime instances as complementary to microVMs rather than a replacement, and encourages mixed topologies where an orchestrator agent on microVMs dispatches long running work to workers on instances. InfoQ has covered the progression of AWS's AgentCore functionality, from the original AgentCore launch, through Agent-to-Agent protocol support for interoperable multi-agent workflows, to the Agent Registry and the Loom reference platform for governed agent deployments.
A few things that should make agent developers smile: your agents can call each other as tools within a shared session, iterating autonomously until the job is done. Sebastien Stormacq
An engineering guide from Enkompass goes deeper into the new capacity provider primitive that underpins runtime instances. A capacity provider defines allowed instance families, operating system, networking and storage, and acts as a contract between agents and the EC2 capacity that AgentCore will provision, patch and scale on their behalf. Teams set bounds such as minimum and maximum instance counts and target utilisation, and then attach one or more agent runtimes to that provider with a session time to live of up to fourteen days, avoiding the need to manage Auto Scaling groups, launch templates or AMI pipelines directly.
Enkompass also stresses that runtime instances are best suited to workloads that need longer than eight hours of continuous runtime, require GPUs or large memory footprints, or benefit from several agents co-located on the same host for tight collaboration. The microVM based runtime remains the default choice for short, bursty, request response style agents, because it starts quickly, isolates sessions and bills per second on actual CPU and peak memory up to eight hours. The guide expects most organisations to run both models side by side, placing high volume, short lived traffic on microVMs and reserving instances for a smaller set of long running, stateful or accelerator heavy workloads that previously forced teams to maintain separate EC2 fleets.
A cost analysis from eCorpIT focuses on the financial trade offs between runtime instances and microVMs. Runtime instances are billed at standard EC2 rates for the chosen instance type in the customers account, plus a management fee. In contrast, microVMs charge per vCPU hour and per GB hour with no separate management fee, and can be cheaper for agents with low sustained CPU utilisation and long idle gaps. The cost analysis suggests a break even at roughly 24% sustained CPU utilisation for runtime instances, before any Savings Plan discounts. Because runtime instances run in the customers account, EC2 commitment discounts such as Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply to the compute portion but not to the management fee. The article argues that co-locating several agents on a single host and stopping sessions when work completes are the main levers for keeping instance based costs under control.
Community reactions have highlighted these integration points. A short analysis on Four Signals describes runtime instances as a major infrastructure launch aligned with the rise of agent orchestration platforms and notes the hybrid pattern of microVM orchestrators dispatching work to instance based workers. A summary on daily.dev emphasises the fourteen day session limit, shared file systems and support for popular agent frameworks as key practical benefits for development teams. On LinkedIn, engineer Kosti Vasilakakis noted that runtime instances reuse the same AgentCore APIs and session pinning model that existing teams already use, reducing friction in adopting the new compute type.
Microsoft has taken a similar approach through Azure Foundry hosted agents. These provision per-session virtual machine sandboxes with persistent home directories and file storage, restoring state automatically when sessions resume after idle periods or restarts. The documentation describes how the service supports multi-agent runs with managed lifecycles across Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot.
AWS documentation is available at the AgentCore runtime instance page.

articles.title: Google Pixel 11 vs Pixel 11 Pro Compared
articles.text:
Table of contents
Google’s Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro share a lot on paper. Both phones have a 6.3-inch display, the new Tensor G6 chip, 256GB of base storage, 12GB of RAM at their cheapest configuration, Android 17, and seven years of software updates. Their dimensions are almost identical too.
The price tells a different story. The Pixel 11 starts at $899, while the Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099. In the UK, they start at £879 and £1,079. That $200 gap raises one clear question: what do you get for the extra money?
Most of that premium goes into a better screen, stronger camera hardware, and a handful of Pro-only features. The processor and most of the software stay the same on both phones. Here is how the Pixel 11 vs Pixel 11 Pro comparison breaks down.
Pixel 11 vs Pixel 11 Pro specs at a glance
| Spec | Pixel 11 | Pixel 11 Pro | 
| Display | 6.3-inch OLED, 1080 x 2424, 60-120Hz | 6.3-inch LTPO OLED, 1280 x 2856, 1-120Hz | 
| Peak brightness | Up to 3,000 nits | Up to 3,600 nits | 
| Processor | Tensor G6 | Tensor G6 | 
| RAM | 12GB | 12GB on 256GB, 16GB on 512GB and 1TB | 
| Storage | 256GB or 512GB | 256GB, 512GB, or 1TB | 
| Main camera | 48MP, 1/1.56-inch sensor | 50MP, 1/1.3-inch sensor | 
| Ultrawide camera | 13MP | 48MP | 
| Telephoto camera | 10.8MP, 5x optical | 48MP, 5x optical | 
| Max zoom | 30x | 120x | 
| Selfie camera | 10.5MP | 42MP | 
| Battery | 4,985mAh | 4,850mAh | 
| Wireless charging | Up to 25W Qi2.2 | Up to 25W Qi2.2 | 
| Weight | 197g | 204g | 
| Starting price | $899 / £879 | $1,099 / £1,079 | 
A few differences stand out from that table:
- The Pro has a sharper, brighter screen that can drop as low as 1Hz to save power.
- The camera hardware is much stronger on the Pro, not just a small step up.
- You only get 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage if you buy the higher storage Pro tiers.
- The standard Pixel 11 actually has a bigger battery than the Pro.
Design and display
Picking the Pro does not mean picking a bigger phone. The Pixel 11 measures 152.8 x 72 x 8.6mm and weighs 197g. The Pro measures 152.7 x 71.9 x 8.4mm and weighs 204g. Both use Gorilla Glass Victus 2 and carry an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance.
Google gives the two phones different finishes. The Pixel 11 pairs a polished glass back with a satin aluminum frame. The Pro uses a matte glass back with a mostly polished aluminum frame, plus an extra scratch-resistant coating on the screen.
The display is where the gap grows. The Pixel 11 runs a 1080 x 2424 OLED panel at 60 to 120Hz. The Pro steps up to a 1280 x 2856 LTPO OLED that can scale from 1Hz to 120Hz, which helps it save battery on static screens. Pixel density goes from 422ppi on the Pixel 11 to 495ppi on the Pro.
Google also rates the Pro brighter: up to 3,600 nits peak versus 3,000 nits on the standard model. These are manufacturer figures for now. Independent brightness and color accuracy tests should give a clearer picture once reviewers get retail units.
For everyday indoor use, the Pixel 11’s 120Hz screen already covers the basics well. The Pro display makes more sense if you want sharper text, a lower minimum refresh rate, or the highest brightness Google offers this year.
Performance and software
Both phones run on the same Tensor G6 chip with a Titan M3 security coprocessor. Google says the new chip brings faster web browsing and quicker app launches than the Tensor G5, along with faster on-device AI processing that uses less power. These are Google’s own figures and still need independent testing to confirm.
RAM is where things get interesting. A 256GB Pixel 11 has 12GB of RAM. So does a 256GB Pixel 11 Pro. The Pro only moves up to 16GB once you choose the 512GB or 1TB tier. The regular Pixel 11 stays at 12GB even at 512GB.
Software support is the same on both phones. Each launches on Android 17 and gets seven years of OS, security, and Pixel Drop updates. Both also carry Google’s current Gemini features.
The Pro adds a few hardware extras. HiLight uses colored LEDs on the back to show notifications when your phone is face down. Connectivity also moves up, from Wi-Fi 6E on the Pixel 11 to Wi-Fi 7 on the Pro, which also includes UWB support.
Cameras
This is where the two phones separate the most.
The Pixel 11 has a 48MP main camera with a 1/1.56-inch sensor and an f/1.70 lens. The Pro uses a larger 1/1.3-inch, 50MP sensor with an f/1.68 lens.
The gap widens on the other lenses. The Pixel 11’s ultrawide camera is 13MP with an f/2.2 lens. The Pro’s ultrawide jumps to 48MP with a brighter f/1.7 lens and autofocus. Both phones offer 5x optical zoom, but the Pixel 11’s telephoto sensor is a small 10.8MP unit, while the Pro uses a much larger 48MP sensor.
The selfie cameras show the same pattern. The Pixel 11 has a 10.5MP front camera, and the Pro moves up to 42MP.
Zoom range tells its own story. The Pixel 11 tops out at 30x digital zoom. The Pro reaches 120x. The Pro also adds Pro Controls, 50MP high-resolution capture, Instant Night Sight, Video Boost, Night Sight Video, and Pro Stable Video. It can record 8K video through Video Boost, while the Pixel 11 caps out at 4K60.
These specs make the Pro the clearly more capable camera phone on paper. How big the difference looks in your own photos will depend on independent camera tests once retail units are out.
Battery and charging
The battery numbers hold a surprise. The Pixel 11 has a 4,985mAh battery, which is bigger than the Pro’s 4,850mAh cell. That is a 135mAh gap in favor of the cheaper phone. Google still rates both phones for more than 30 hours of use.
The Pro’s LTPO screen can drop to 1Hz, which may help it close that gap through lower power draw. The Pixel 11, on the other hand, pushes fewer pixels overall. Which phone actually lasts longer in daily use will only become clear once independent battery tests are published.
Charging is tied on paper. Both phones can reach up to 55% in about 30 minutes with a 30W or higher USB-C charger, and both support Qi2.2 wireless charging at up to 25W.
Price
The Pixel 11 starts at $899 for 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. The 512GB version costs $1,019. The Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099 for 256GB, rises to $1,219 for 512GB with 16GB of RAM, and reaches $1,499 for the 1TB model.
| Model | US price | UK price | 
| Pixel 11, 256GB | $899 | £879 | 
| Pixel 11, 512GB | $1,019 | not listed | 
| Pixel 11 Pro, 256GB | $1,099 | £1,079 | 
| Pixel 11 Pro, 512GB | $1,219 | not listed | 
| Pixel 11 Pro, 1TB | $1,499 | not listed | 
At matching storage tiers, the Pro costs $200 more. At 512GB, that $200 also buys you an extra 4GB of RAM. 256GB, it does not, since both phones carry 12GB there.
UK pricing follows the same pattern, with a £200 gap between the two starting prices.
Google has not listed Nigeria, Kenya, or South Africa as official Google Store markets for the Pixel 11 series. Prices in these markets typically come through import retailers rather than direct Google sales, so treat any currency conversion of the US price as a rough guide rather than the actual retail cost. Import duties, shipping, and retailer margins usually push local prices higher than a straight conversion suggests.
Pixel 11 vs Pixel 11 Pro: Which should you buy
For most buyers, the Pixel 11 looks like the smarter place to start. You get the same Tensor G6 chip, the same seven years of updates, a 5x optical zoom camera, and the same fast wireless charging for $200 less.
Buy the Pixel 11 if you want:
- The same Tensor G6 chip and Android 17 software as the Pro
- A 5x optical zoom camera that covers most everyday shots
- 256GB of storage at the lowest price
- Fast Qi2.2 wireless charging without paying extra
Buy the Pixel 11 Pro if you want:
- A sharper, brighter screen that can scale down to 1Hz
- Much stronger main, ultrawide, and telephoto cameras
- A 42MP selfie camera and zoom up to 120x
- Wi-Fi 7, UWB, HiLight, and the option of 16GB RAM or 1TB storage
At 256GB, the choice comes down mostly to how much you care about the camera and screen, since RAM and the processor stay the same. At 512GB, the Pro becomes easier to justify because that same $200 also gets you 16GB of RAM. If you rarely shoot long zoom photos or use advanced video controls, the Pixel 11 gives you most of the experience for less money.
Frequently asked questions
Q) What is the difference between the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro?
A) The main differences lie in the display and cameras. The Pro has a sharper, brighter LTPO screen, much larger ultrawide and telephoto camera sensors, a 42MP selfie camera, and zoom up to 120x. It also adds Wi-Fi 7, UWB, and the option of 16GB RAM or 1TB storage.
Q) Do the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro use the same processor?
A) Yes. Both phones run on Google’s Tensor G6 chip with a Titan M3 security coprocessor.
Q) Is the Pixel 11 Pro camera better than the Pixel 11 camera?
A) The Pro has significantly stronger hardware across its main, ultrawide, telephoto, and selfie cameras, along with extra photo and video modes. How much better your actual photos look will depend on independent camera tests once retail units are available.
Q) Are the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro the same size?
A) They are close. Both have 6.3-inch screens. The Pixel 11 measures 152.8 x 72 x 8.6mm and weighs 197g, while the Pro measures 152.7 x 71.9 x 8.4mm and weighs 204g.
Q) Is the Pixel 11 Pro worth the extra money?
A) The $200 premium makes the most sense if photography, video, or the sharper LTPO display matter to you, or if you need 16GB of RAM or 1TB of storage. If you mainly care about the Tensor G6 chip, Android 17, and Google’s AI features, the Pixel 11 gives you most of that same core experience for less.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: React Router v8: A Deliberately Boring Release with ESM-Only Builds and Default Middleware
articles.text:
React Router, the widely used routing library for React that now underpins the Remix framework, has released React Router v8, shipping on June 17, 2026 with a deliberately small set of breaking changes, modernised baselines, and a commitment to a predictable yearly release cadence.
React Router v8 introduces updated minimum versions, an ESM-only build, middleware enabled by default, and the graduation of several future flags into standard behaviour. It also marks React Router v6 and Remix v2 as End of Life, so neither will receive further security updates.
Writing on the Remix blog, Developer Relations Manager Brooks Lybrand framed the release as intentionally uneventful, explaining that the team's aim for the past several major versions has been to make them "as boring as possible". He added that "it's not a major version if nothing broke", while stressing that every breaking change in v8 is one developers could already adopt in v7 through future flags.
The new baselines are Node 22.22.0+, React 19.2.7+, and Vite 7+. To modernise the library, React Router is now published as an ESM-only module, with tsconfig target and lib fields updated to ES2022. Four future flags, including v8_middleware and v8_viteEnvironmentApi, have been removed and their behaviours made default, while splitRouteModules moves to a top-level config option that is enabled by default.
Middleware becoming a baseline drew particular attention. In a piece titled "React Router v8 Makes Middleware a Baseline", Roman Fedyskyi wrote that the change pushes frontend teams to "centralize auth, logging, headers", arguing that "many frontend incidents are policy incidents". Not all coverage was reassuring, with byteiota warning that "three breaking changes will catch teams off guard" for a package pulling more than 50 million weekly npm downloads.
In his React Router v8 and Beyond talk, Lybrand joked that they "broke all your apps, and we did it just to make you mad", a nod to the sceptical reaction on Reddit. Some developers have already looked elsewhere, with The New Stack reporting that some are turning to TanStack Router after the Remix and React Router merger. TanStack Router remains the main challenger, promoted for its end-to-end type safety and built-in stale-while-revalidate caching, while Next.js continues to lead on React Server Components maturity.
Migration is designed to be straightforward. The official upgrade guide advises updating peer dependencies, adopting the future flags, and removing deprecated APIs before installing. A key deprecation is the removal of the react-router-dom package:
- import { Link, useLocation } from "react-router-dom";
+ import { Link, useLocation } from "react-router";
DOM-specific APIs now import from react-router/dom instead. React Router v8 is already supported on Netlify and by the Sentry SDK, with minor releases up to v8.3.0 following since launch.
React Router is an open-source library developed via an Open Governance model and maintained by the team at Shopify, with upgrade instructions available at reactrouter.com.

articles.title: Xiaomi lanza la campana extractora perfecta: ha solucionado dos problemas de toda la vida
articles.text:
Xiaomi ha vuelto a hacerlo. Acaba de lanzar la renovación de un producto que lleva años estancado y que no parecía tener demasiado margen de mejora. Estábamos equivocados: las campanas extractoras todavía pueden mejorarse, ser más eficientes y contar con tecnologías que las hacen mucho más atractivas. Porque sí, hoy mismo Xiaomi ha presentado la Mijia Smart Smoke Cleaner Pro, un extractor para la cocina que revoluciona el sector y deja al resto de opciones con la cara roja.
Lo ha hecho con la dinámica a la que nos tiene acostumbrados la compañía: un diseño sobrio, elegante y sencillo con un toque tecnológico muy marcado y una relación calidad/precio marca de la casa. Su precio está a la par con el resto de campanas extractoras de gama alta, pero su capacidad, cifras y tecnología se sitúan varios niveles por encima.
Para empezar, Xiaomi ha revolucionado el diseño tradicional de extracción. Esta campana cuenta con dos zonas de succión: la de toda la vida en la parte superior y otra lateral que es la que marca la diferencia. El conjunto, según la compañía, consigue un poder de succión de 1.400 Pa, una cifra récord que, junto con la disposición de las entradas, hace que no se escape nada en ningún tipo de cocción.
Además, tiene varios sensores que le permiten conocer la situación del viento exterior en el punto de extracción para ajustar con precisión la potencia en cada momento. Ahora bien, la joya de la corona está en lo que no se ve a simple vista.
La campana de Xiaomi esconde dos secretos que te van a enamorar
Xiaomi no solo ha rediseñado el formato tradicional de campana extractora para mejorar la succión y que no se escape nada de humo. También ha incluido varios sistemas inteligentes, un motor especial y un conducto de extracción pensado para un solo objetivo: permitir la mayor potencia posible con el menor ruido.
De hecho, Xiaomi presume de tener una de las campanas más potentes del mercado y, a la vez, una de las más silenciosas. La compañía asegura que el ruido está en torno a los 58 decibelios, una cifra bastante baja para su nivel de succión.
Por último, dos características que la convierten en una de las mejores opciones del mercado. Para empezar, cuenta con un sistema interno en el motor para limpiarlo automáticamente de forma periódica y no tener que desmontar nada.
Y hablando de limpieza, tampoco tienes que preocuparte de la grasa y los botones de la campana. Xiaomi ha incluido un sensor que permite encenderla y controlarla con gestos, por lo que no tienes que tocarla cuando tengas las manos sucias.
¿Y su precio? Pues, aunque sigue siendo una campana extractora algo cara, lo cierto es que Xiaomi ha incluido varias tecnologías que la sitúan muy por encima de opciones de gama alta como las de Samsung o LG. Por ahora solo se vende en China por 345 euros.

articles.title: GTA VI keeps leaking ahead of its gameplay premiere
articles.text:
Clips of what appears to be Grand Theft Auto VI have hit the internet, possibly spoiling aspects of the game ahead of Rockstar Games’ deep dive debuting on Netflix next week and its long-awaited launch in November.
GTA VI keeps leaking ahead of its gameplay premiere
Some of the clips seemingly showing Grand Theft Auto VI footage have been pulled.
I’ve seen three clips seemingly showing off the game, though two have been pulled from the site I saw them on “due to a copyright claim.” The first clip (now removed) was a quiet scene that mostly focused on Jason Duval, one the game’s two protagonists, shooting a basketball into a hoop. Another clip (also removed) featured more of the crime-focused gameplay you’d expect from GTA, including Duval hitting a person with a wrench, and also showed the return of a six-star Wanted system.
A third clip, which is live as I write this, shows Duval driving at night, punching some people, using a taser, and stealing a truck. The clip then jumps to what looks like a cutscene from a different part of the game in the daytime.
The videos were watermarked by a person or group identifying themselves as “CyberLeek.” The third clip has a call for viewers to buy a CyberLeek cryptocurrency, a QR code, links to some sketchy-looking CyberLeek URLs, and a statement that says “NO PHYSICAL DISCS? THEN MORE LEEKS!”, which is seemingly a reference to Rockstar’s decision not to launch GTA VI on a physical disc.
This isn’t the first time apparent footage from GTA VI has leaked. In 2022, 90 videos leaked online long before the game’s official reveal more than a year later (a reveal that also leaked, leading Rockstar to publish the game’s first trailer a day early). A teen who played a key role in leaking the 90 videos was sentenced to life in a secure hospital. Rockstar also confirmed earlier this year that it had data compromised in a hack of a third-party provider, but said the incident would have “no impact on our organization or our players.”
Rockstar and owner Take-Two didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. The GTA VI “extended look” premieres on Netflix on August 27th at 3PM ET and will stream on YouTube at 9PM ET. The $79.99 title is scheduled to launch on November 19th, and for the most part, the industry is steering clear of November and launching their big games earlier in the year.

articles.title: Home batteries are suddenly cheap and everywhere. Here’s why. | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Competition is heating up in the race to install home battery systems, with heavy hitters and nimble startups all vying for a piece of the market.
Tesla may have led the pack for years, but recently it has been feeling the heat from upstarts like Base Power, which has raised $2 billion in less than a year. The automaker-cum-energy company recently introduced a new Powerwall battery leasing plan that cuts the monthly price by more than two-thirds, an apparent response to all that competition.
Just how steep is that price cut? Home batteries typically cost more than $10,000 installed, making them attractive only to people with deep pockets who already have solar panels generating more power than they can use. But now, homeowners in Texas can lease either 27 kilowatt-hours’ of worth of Tesla Powerwalls for $35 per month or 39.2 kilowatt-hours of Base Power batteries for $19.
That kind of pricing is only possible because of two things: declining battery costs, and a technology known as the virtual power plant (VPP). A VPP aggregates and coordinates distributed energy resources like batteries and, in some cases, water heaters so that thousands of individual devices behave on the grid like a single large power plant, one that a utility can call on when it needs extra electricity. Companies like Tesla and Base Power, for example, can use their battery fleets as a VPP to help utilities and grid operators fill in gaps during periods of high demand.
The market for this technology is still small — $7.4 billion today — but it’s expected to top $30 billion by 2033, according to Grandview Research.
Traditionally, to handle spikes in demand, utilities have had two options: build expensive, specialized power plants known as “peaker plants,” which only run during periods of high demand, or pay large energy users, like factories, to disconnect for a few hours. Now, they can pay a VPP instead.
VPP operators charge the batteries when electricity rates are low, then sell that stored power back to the grid at a profit when demand sends prices soaring. The operator pockets a chunk of those profits, passing some on to consumers in the form of low electricity prices, cheap backup batteries, or both.
“There are resiliency needs everywhere,” Tim Pianta, head of utility partnerships at Base Power, told TechCrunch. “Our goal is to have it be a win-win, like it’s a no brainer.”
As electricity demand rises on the back of AI data centers and the electrification of the economy, utilities and grid operators are embracing VPPs with newfound fervor.
VPPs also have a speed advantage. Unlike building a peaker power plant, which can take years, VPPs can be built in months since installing batteries in people’s homes eliminates many land, permitting, and interconnection headaches. Base Power has a deal with CoServ, a North Texas electricity cooperative, to build a 100 megawatt VPP, for example. A traditional 100-megawatt power plant would take two to four years to come online, Pianta said. “We’re on pace to install that in under 12 months.”
Because VPPs rely on assets like batteries that are spread out across the grid, near where people actually use electricity, utilities don’t have to spend as much building new power lines and other infrastructure to support them, either.
It wasn’t always obvious that VPPs could play a key role in the grid. For years, Tesla operated a VPP using its Powerwall fleet, but it didn’t market it that way to consumers. Instead, Tesla encouraged homeowners to use their batteries for arbitrage with their electricity supply, charging their batteries with cheap, excess solar power during the day and drawing them down at night.
It worked well enough to get more than 6.7 gigawatts’ worth of Powerwalls installed, but newcomers like Base Power and its monthly battery plan are pushing Tesla to change tack. Base Power has been installing 8 megawatt-hours’ worth of batteries every day, a rate it hopes to double by the end of the year.
“We’ve always anticipated competition to come into the space,” Pianta said. “We wouldn’t have started a company if we didn’t think there was a really big opportunity here.”
Software gives VPPs another edge. Utility-scale batteries, which are VPPs’ closest competitor, are at a disadvantage because they have to connect directly to the grid, which means dealing with congestion and long wait times to connect to it. “A distributed storage solution is able to clear both of those hurdles,” Pianta said.
While VPPs are gaining traction in a few markets like Texas and California, they’re likely to spread nationwide in the coming years as data centers look for ways to connect to the grid faster, said Nicole Tomasin, chief commercial officer at Energy Access Innovations.
“As we see more hyperscalers, more data centers coming online, I think more [VPP] programs are going to be accelerated because we’re accelerating demand,” she told TechCrunch. “They’re not buying kilowatt-hours, they’re buying interconnect speed at that point. A distributed fleet can be assembled in months against a queue that takes years.”

articles.title: Electronic Health Record Implementation: Key Steps, Costs, and Best Practices - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Adding software to a clinic is not like updating a phone app. A proper electronic health record implementation represents a deep operational, clinical, and technical overhaul that reshapes daily care delivery. It alters how doctors write notes, how nurses record vitals, and how billers process claims. (It is rarely easy.)
To succeed, health systems must master the software rollout lifecycle, manage expenses, and follow proven electronic health record implementation best practices from day one.
What Does EHR Implementation Involve?
Buying software is simple. Paying the vendor invoice takes five minutes. However, a complete EMR implementation demands far more than purchasing user licenses or turning on basic system settings. It requires total coordination across clinical workflows, legacy data migration, IT infrastructure, user security protocols, and human behavior.
If you are implementing an EHR, you are essentially redesigning how an entire healthcare institution functions. Doctors must adjust their charting routines—often while talking face-to-face with patients. Nurses need clear digital protocols for entering patient vitals without adding ten extra clicks. Meanwhile, IT security leads must safeguard patient privacy while ensuring that clinical records flow safely across departments. Without tight coordination across every team, even the most expensive technology platform will fail to deliver real value. So, treat this as a human operational project first, and a technical upgrade second.
Electronic Health Record Implementation: Key Steps From Planning to Go-Live
Navigating the core rollout lifecycle requires a disciplined, step-by-step approach. The essential EHR implementation steps begin with defining organizational goals and mapping daily clinical workflows. From there, execution teams transition into data migration, system integration, rigorous stress testing, hands-on staff training, and official go-live deployment. Technical readiness alone will not guarantee a smooth launch. System configuration and clinical adoption must move forward together in lockstep. If clinicians cannot navigate the interface comfortably on launch day, patient care stalls, wait times skyrocket, and severe staff burnout quickly follows. Balance is necessary.
Planning, EHR Selection, and Workflow Design
Every solid technology project starts on paper. Long before writing custom code or signing vendor software agreements, leadership teams must draft a comprehensive EHR implementation plan outline. This initial planning document establishes project scope, assigns clear management responsibilities, identifies privacy compliance needs, and defines essential interoperability requirements across departments.
Next comes current-state workflow mapping. Project leaders must carefully analyze how patient information currently moves through clinics, from initial patient check-in to final discharge.
When implementing EHR systems, healthcare executives frequently make the fatal mistake of leaving bedside clinicians out of early system design sessions. That is a huge error. Physicians and nurses know exactly where operational bottlenecks occur—and where care processes break down under shift pressure. (They experience it every single day.) Involving clinicians early ensures the new platform mirrors actual care delivery rather than theoretical administrative guidelines. Redesigning workflows around real clinical routines prevents post-launch anger, reduces redundant mouse clicks, and keeps patient safety front and center.
Data Migration, Integration, Testing, Training, and Go-Live
Once planning ends, execution begins in earnest. The practical stages of EHR implementation center heavily on data preparation, system integration, configuration validation, and comprehensive user education. Legacy patient charts must be cleansed, standardized, and migrated into the new platform without dropping key historical details or allergy records. At the same time, software engineers build secure data channels connecting the platform to external lab software, pharmacy databases, and billing networks.
Then comes testing. Never skip end-to-end clinical simulations. Testing individual features isolated in a lab is not enough—you must validate entire patient care workflows under peak network stress.
Finally, organization-wide training prepares hospital personnel for launch. When implementing an EMR, user confidence dictates operational success. Staff members need role-based, interactive instruction tailored directly to their actual duties. (Generic recorded webinars rarely work.) Providing hands-on, shoulder-to-shoulder support during go-live gives doctors and nurses a safety net, keeping stress manageable and preventing severe patient care delays during those crucial launch weeks.
How Much Does EHR Implementation Cost?
Budgeting for modern health software is notoriously tricky. The overall financial commitment of electronic medical records implementation extends well past basic software licensing or cloud subscription fees.
Healthcare entities must account for professional consulting services, custom system configuration, legacy data extraction, and physical IT infrastructure upgrades. Third-party software integrations—such as linking to regional lab networks or specialized radiology software—introduce additional technical fees. Ongoing project management, security compliance auditing, and extensive usability testing also require substantial capital allocation.
However, the largest hidden expense often comes from temporary productivity disruption. Patient charting takes longer during the initial transition phase, which reduces daily patient volume and cuts short-term clinical revenue.
Total capital expenditures vary dramatically based on institutional scale. A small independent clinic might spend tens of thousands of dollars, whereas a multi-hospital regional health system can easily spend tens of millions. Ultimately, the total budget for any implementation of EHR depends on organization size, scope of customization, legacy data volume, and interoperability complexity. Skimping on user training or data preparation to save money almost always leads to massive financial losses later.
Common EHR Implementation Challenges
Even well-funded healthcare initiatives routinely run into serious friction. The implementation of electronic medical records in hospitals frequently hits roadblocks like staff resistance, dirty data, complex system integration, and underestimated project scope.
Why do clinical workers resist? Organizational change is mentally exhausting. When new software slows down veteran doctors, severe frustration builds rapidly across departments. If system training is brief or overly academic, clinicians feel unprepared and abandoned.
Technical hurdles create major operational headaches too. Migrating low-quality data—such as duplicate patient profiles or incomplete medication histories—corrupts the new database instantly. Integration failures between disparate medical systems cause severe clinical delays, forcing nurses to enter patient data manually across multiple screens. (This invites human error.)
Unclear administrative ownership compounds these pain points. Without explicit decision-making authority, timelines drift, project scope creeps out of control, and budgets balloon quickly. Addressing these operational vulnerabilities early protects project deadlines, preserves clinician morale, and prevents catastrophic patient care disruptions when system launch day arrives.
Best Practices for a Successful EHR Implementation
Mitigating major operational risk requires strategic discipline. Executing proven, successful EHR implementation strategies bridges the gap between software launch and genuine clinical adoption across hospital units.
Follow these ten essential steps to guide your deployment:
- Executive Governance: Establish clear steering committees to enforce project accountability.
- Clinician Involvement: Engage frontline physicians and nurses in software design from day one.
- Workflow Redesign: Optimize daily clinical processes before locking in permanent software rules.
- Realistic Budgeting and Scheduling: Account for productivity dips and build timeline buffers.
- Data Preparation: Cleanse and validate legacy health records prior to system migration.
- Interoperability Planning: Build secure connections across all internal and external health systems.
- Full Workflow Testing: Execute realistic clinical stress simulations under peak traffic load.
- Role-Based Training: Deliver tailored, hands-on instruction for specific medical roles.
- At-the-Elbow Go-Live Support: Deploy expert super-users to assist clinical staff directly.
- Performance Monitoring: Track post-launch adoption metrics and resolve software bugs quickly.
By prioritizing staff readiness and process alignment, healthcare institutions avoid widespread operational chaos and protect patient safety throughout transition.
What Happens After EHR Go-Live?
Crossing the official software launch finish line is not the end of the journey. Go-live is simply the beginning of long-term operational refinement. Healthcare institutions must transition smoothly from initial deployment mode into continuous system optimization.
During the immediate post-launch phase, dedicated technical support teams resolve emergent software bugs, monitor interface stability, and deploy crucial security updates. User workflows will still need active adjustment. As doctors and nurses gain familiarity with the digital platform, they discover new opportunities to eliminate unnecessary steps and streamline daily charting routines. Ongoing, role-based education helps staff master advanced software features, preventing poor documentation habits from taking root across clinical departments.
Regular performance measurement keeps the platform aligned with strategic organizational goals. Tracking key operational metrics—like chart completion speed, billing accuracy, and patient wait times—highlights where technical tweaks or additional staff coaching are necessary. True long-term success comes from viewing your electronic health record implementation as a continuous commitment to clinical excellence rather than a simple, one-time IT installation.

articles.title: Google Agenda ajoute enfin le bouton qu'on attendait pour bloquer les spams
articles.text:
Marre de voir votre calendrier pollué par des réunions ou les sollicitations incessantes d’un collègue insistant ? Google propose depuis ce mardi 18 août 2026 un nouvel outil qui permet de bannir un utilisateur pour faire un peu de ménage dans votre agenda.
Nettoyez votre Google Agenda en quelques clics
Si vous bloquez une personne sur Google Agenda, l’événement en cours est automatiquement supprimé et l’expéditeur ne peut plus vous faire parvenir la moindre invitation. Une solution radicale qui s’adresse aux utilisateurs d’un compte Google, mais aussi aux expéditeurs externes ne passant pas par Google Agenda. Dans ce dernier cas, la procédure passe par un blocage direct dans Gmail en stoppant les courriels tout en empêchant la création d’événements associés.
Bannir un contact ajoute ainsi automatiquement ce dernier à la liste noire de l’ensemble de votre compte. Les interactions avec la personne ciblée se retrouvent donc bloquées sur l’ensemble des services Google pris en charge. La réciproque s’applique également, un utilisateur déjà bloqué sur une autre plateforme comme Gmail verra ses invitations Agenda immédiatement filtrées.
Un déploiement progressif pour les utilisateurs Google Workspace
Si vous êtes administrateur pour une entreprise, aucune configuration préalable n’est requise puisque la fonction ne dispose d’aucun contrôle admin dédié. Les utilisateurs finaux peuvent gérer leurs paramètres en toute autonomie grâce à la documentation mise en ligne par le support technique. Cela simplifie la prise en main sans intervention technique particulière.
À lire : Google Agenda ajoute une nouveauté que vous allez utiliser tous les jours
Côté disponibilité, cette nouveauté s’adresse aux clients Google Workspace (Entreprise et individuel). Lancé le 18 août 2026 pour les domaines en Rapid Release et Scheduled Release, le déploiement est comme toujours progressif. Il faudra ainsi compter jusqu’à 15 jours pour voir l’option apparaître sur l’ensemble des comptes éligibles.

articles.title: Dune 3 propose 71 minutes d'images au format élargi exclusives aux salles IMAX
articles.text:
Le débat qui agite les cinéphiles ne porte plus seulement sur le scénario ou l’interprétation de Timothée Chalamet dans Dune 3, mais sur la géométrie pure de l’écran. Alors que les cinémas vendent leurs tickets au tarif fort, la différence d’expérience d’une salle à l’autre n’a jamais été aussi brutale. Aller voir le final d’Arrakis sans choisir le bon projecteur, c’est sciemment décider de regarder un chef-d’œuvre à travers le trou d’une serrure.
1,43:1 : La verticale du désert tout simplement amputée pour Dune 3
Dans les rares complexes équipés en IMAX Laser et sur les mythiques écrans en IMAX 70mm argentique, ces 71 minutes de métrage basculeront dans le ratio vertical maximal de 1,43:1.
- 40 % d’image découpée aux ciseaux : dans une salle conventionnelle, le film reste bloqué dans son format panoramique horizontal (2,39:1). Les bandes noires supérieures et inférieures viennent couper l’image en haut et en bas.
- L’échelle monumentale réduite à zéro : la taille titanesque des vers de sable, les vertiges de la géographie d’Arrakis et le gigantisme des structures architecturales perdent leur pouvoir d’écrasement dès lors que le cadre est tronqué.
Avec l’arrivée du chef opérateur Linus Sandgren (La La Land, No Time to Die) à la photographie, qui reprend le flambeau avec un tournage direct en pellicule 65mm, Denis Villeneuve pousse le soin de la lumière et du grain à son niveau le plus extrême. Priver ces séquences du format 1,43:1 natif revient littéralement à couper les bords d’un tableau de maître pour le faire entrer dans un cadre trop petit. C’est dommage et c’est même un peu triste comme choix marketing initial.
Le faux débat du Dolby Vision et le piège des grands écrans
Certains spectateurs hésitent encore à délaisser la promesse du Dolby Cinema pour privilégier l’IMAX. Mais le calcul est mauvais. Même si le traitement Dolby Vision offre une profondeur des noirs inouïe et une saturation des couleurs éclatante, les salles Dolby restent désespérément coincées dans un format fixe. Elles ne bénéficieront pas de la magie des transitions où l’écran s’ouvre soudainement vers le haut pour engloutir le spectateur.
Quant aux salles géantes classiques (type grand écran panoramique standard) : projeter la majeure partie du film (en 2,20:1) sur une toile extra-large donne l’illusion de la grandeur. Mais il manque l’essentiel : le basculement dynamique. Vous obtenez une grande image plate, mais vous manquez l’effet de souffle propre au format IMAX. Bref, le voir en IMAX va rendre Dune 3 plus bluffant, et 71 minutes inédites, c’est beaucoup.
